docs.title: AIA User Manual
docs.text:
AIA ("AI Assistant") is a command-line program for working with large language models from your terminal. You keep your prompts as plain Markdown files, and AIA fills them in, sends them to the model of your choice, and gives you the answer, or keeps the conversation going in an interactive chat.

This manual covers AIA 2.0.0.

docs.title: Who this manual is for
docs.text: You use a terminal every day and you want an LLM to be part of that work, not a browser tab off to the side. You don't need to know Ruby to use AIA. Some optional features (ERB templates, custom tools) use Ruby, and the manual explains what you need when you get there.

docs.title: What you can do with AIA
docs.text:
• Keep a library of prompts. Each prompt is a .md file in your prompts directory (~/.prompts by default). You run one by name: aia code_review.
  • Fill in prompts with parameters. A prompt can declare values such as language or audience. AIA asks for them when you run it.
  • Feed it your files and your shell. Pass files on the command line, pipe text in on stdin, or embed $(git diff) in a prompt and AIA runs the command for you.
  • Chat. aia --chat opens an interactive session. Use / directives in the chat to switch models, include files, save checkpoints, and more.
  • Use any model. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and the other providers RubyLLM supports, plus local models through Ollama or LM Studio. Pick one per run with --model.
  • Run several models at once. --model gpt-4o,claude-sonnet-4-5 sends the same prompt to both. Add --consensus and AIA combines their answers into one.
  • Chain prompts into pipelines. One prompt's output becomes the next one's input.
  • Give the model tools. Load Ruby tools or connect MCP servers so the model can read files, query APIs, or run commands, with your approval.
  • Track usage. --tokens and --cost show token counts, time and cost after every response.

docs.title: A taste
docs.text:
# Ask a one-off question by piping it in
echo "Explain the difference between a process and a thread in two sentences." | aia

# Run a saved prompt against a file
aia summarize meeting_notes.txt

# Start a chat, with a role, on a specific model
aia --chat --role code_reviewer --model claude-sonnet-4-5

docs.title: How this manual is organized
docs.text:
Part What it covers Getting Started Installation, a Quick Tour of the main features, and Your First Prompt. Start here if you are new. Everyday Use Running prompts, chat sessions, context files and piping, roles and skills, choosing models, and output, history and usage reports. Writing Prompts Prompt files and front matter, parameters, directives, ERB and shell expansion, pipelines, and executable prompts. Extending AIA Tools, MCP servers, multiple models and consensus, crews, local models, images and speech, and advanced modes. Configuration The config file, environment variables, how settings override each other, and security. Reference Every command-line option, every directive, every configuration key, and the FAQ and troubleshooting page. Appendix Upgrading to 2.0, migrating old prompts, and a glossary.

The Getting Started and Everyday Use parts are written to be read in order. The rest you can dip into when you need it.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The terms this manual uses, in alphabetical order, with a pointer to where each is explained.

@mention Writing @name in a chat message to send it to a particular crew member, or @crew to send it to all of them. See Crews. Chat session An interactive conversation started with --chat. The model remembers earlier turns until you /clear them. See Chat Sessions. Checkpoint A named point in a chat conversation, saved with /checkpoint, that you can go back to with /restore. See Chat Sessions. Chief The lead robot of a crew — the one that answers when you don't address anyone in particular. See Crews. Config file The YAML file holding your default settings, ~/.config/aia/aia.yml. A project can add ./config/aia.yml, and -c FILE substitutes another. See The Config File. Consensus With several models, an extra step that merges their answers into one response (--consensus). See Multi-Model & Consensus. Context file A file named on the command line after the prompt ID. Its contents are sent along with the prompt. See Context Files & Piping. Crew The team of robots behind a chat session. Every chat is a crew, even with one model; you add members with /add_recruit. See Crews. Directive A command that starts with /, such as /model, /clear or /webpage. You type directives in chat; some also work inside prompt files. aia handles them itself rather than sending them to the model. See Directives and the Directives reference. ERB Embedded Ruby — <%= … %> tags in a prompt file that are replaced with the result of Ruby code. Parameters and include are written this way. See ERB & Shell. Executable prompt A prompt file whose first line is a #! line that runs aia, so you can run the file directly like a script. See Executable Prompts. Front matter The YAML block between --- lines at the top of a prompt file. It holds the description, parameters, next: / pipeline: and other settings. See Prompt Files. History file The file that keeps the lines you type at the chat prompt, for up-arrow recall. Default ~/.prompts/_prompts.log. See Output & History. MCP (Model Context Protocol) An open protocol for giving models access to tools and data provided by separate programs or services. See MCP Servers. MCP server A program (run locally over stdio) or a web service (over Streamable HTTP) that offers tools through MCP. Configured under mcp_servers: or with --mcp. See MCP Servers. Model The LLM that answers, such as gpt-4o-mini (the default) or claude-sonnet-4-6. Chosen with -m. See Choosing Models. Multi-model Running the same prompt on several models at once, by giving -m a comma-separated list. See Multi-Model & Consensus. Output file The file each response is written to, as well as the terminal. Default temp.md in the current directory; change it with -o or turn it off with --no-output. See Output & History. Parameter A named blank in a prompt, written <%= name %> and declared in the front matter. aia asks you for a value when the parameter has no default. See Parameters. Pipeline A sequence of prompts run one after another in the same conversation, so each sees the responses before it. Built with -p, -n, or next: / pipeline: in front matter. See Pipelines. Plugin A Ruby file in your plugins directory that aia loads at startup and reloads when it changes during a chat. See Plugins. Prompt The text you send to the model. In aia it usually comes from a prompt file, but it can also be piped in or typed in chat. Prompt file A Markdown file (.md) in your prompts directory that contains a prompt, optionally with front matter, parameters, ERB and shell expansion. See Prompt Files. Prompt ID A prompt file's name without .md. aia code_review runs ~/.prompts/code_review.md. A prompt in a subfolder includes the folder (dev/code-review), and an ID starting with /, ./, ../ or ~/ is a path to a prompt file. See Prompt Files. Prompts directory Where aia looks for prompt files. Default ~/.prompts; change it with --prompts-dir or AIA_PROMPTS__DIR. Provider The service or local server that runs a model: openai, anthropic, gemini, ollama, lms and so on. aia --list-providers lists them. See Choosing Models. Provider prefix A provider name written in front of a model name, as in ollama/llama3.2, to say which provider should run it. Recruit A crew member you add with /add_recruit. It stays for the rest of the session and answers to @name. See Crews. Robot aia's name for one configured model connection — a model plus its role, tools and conversation. A chat session has at least one (the chief). Role A prompt file in the roles directory (~/.prompts/roles/) that tells the model who to be, such as "senior Ruby reviewer". Applied with -r. See Roles & Skills. Shell expansion Replacing $(command) in a prompt file with the command's output, and $NAME with an environment variable, before the prompt is sent. See ERB & Shell. Skill A reusable set of instructions stored as a directory containing a SKILL.md file, added to a prompt or chat with -s. See Roles & Skills. Specialist A one-shot robot created with /spawn to handle the next prompt only. See Crews. System prompt Standing instructions given to the model before the conversation. In chat, aia builds it from --system-prompt, the role and any skills. Thinking Reasoning that some models write inside <think>…</think> tags before answering. Hidden unless you pass --thinking. Token The unit models count text in — roughly three-quarters of an English word. Limits and prices are in tokens; --tokens and --cost show usage. Tool A function the model can call to act or look something up — read a file, search the web, query a database. Tools come from Ruby files (--tools), gems (--require) or MCP servers. See Tools. Tool approval The check aia applies before running tools from an MCP server marked requires_approval:. Controlled by --tool-approval. See Security. Tool filter Automatic narrowing of the tools offered to the model on each turn to those relevant to your prompt. On by default; --no-auto-tool-filter turns it off. TrakFlow A task-tracking tool aia can use to record pipelines (--track-pipeline) and plans (/plan, /task, /tasks). See Advanced Modes.

docs.title: Migrating Prompts
docs.text: If your prompts are still in the old two-file format — a .txt file with [PLACEHOLDERS] and //directives, plus a .json file of past parameter values — this page shows how to convert them to the current single-file .md format with the migrate_prompts script.

docs.title: Old format vs. new format
docs.text:
Before: ~/.prompts/summarize.txt …

# ~/.prompts/summarize.txt
# Desc: Summarize the given document
//config temperature 0.3
//include shared_context.md

Summarize the following [DOCUMENT_TYPE] document
for a [TARGET AUDIENCE] reader:

[CONTENT]

… and ~/.prompts/summarize.json, which held the values you'd typed before:

{ "[DOCUMENT_TYPE]": ["report", "article", "paper"], "[CONTENT]": [] }

After: ~/.prompts/summarize.md, exactly as the script writes it:

---
name: summarize
description: Summarize the given document
temperature: 0.3
parameters:
  document_type: paper
  target_audience: null
  content: null
---

<%= include('shared_context.md') %>

Summarize the following <%= document_type %> document
for a <%= target_audience %> reader:

<%= content %>

Settings move into YAML front matter, placeholders become ERB, and each parameter gets a default (null means aia will ask for it).

The script puts each //config setting where aia 2.0 reads it. model, temperature, top_p, next, pipeline, shell and erb stay at the top level of the front matter; everything else goes under a config: key, at its place in the configuration (//config tokens true becomes config: / flags: / tokens: true). A key the script doesn't recognize, such as the removed terse, is put under config: as written and listed as a warning, so you can fix or delete it. See Prompt Files and Parameters.

The script turns //config model … into a front-matter model:, and //temperature / //top_p into temperature: / top_p:. These keep working in 2.0. See Prompt Files.

docs.title: Get the script
docs.text:
migrate_prompts is not installed with the gem. It lives in the aia repository and needs nothing but Ruby:

git clone https://github.com/MadBomber/aia.git
cd aia
ruby bin/migrate_prompts --help

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Always start with a dry run. With no file arguments it scans your whole prompts directory ($AIA_PROMPTS__DIR, or ~/.prompts), including subdirectories:

$ ruby bin/migrate_prompts --dry-run --verbose
Scanning /Users/you/.prompts
Processing 2 .txt file(s)
  Flag: review.txt → review.txt-review (needs review)
  Migrate: summarize.txt → summarize.md
    YAML config keys: temperature
    Parameters: document_type, target_audience, content
    Description: Summarize the given document

Migration summary:
  Migrated:           1 files
  Flagged for review: 1 files (*.txt-review)
  Skipped:            0 files (*.md already exists)

Nothing is changed in a dry run. When the plan looks right, run it for real:

ruby bin/migrate_prompts

Or limit it to particular files or directories:

ruby bin/migrate_prompts ~/.prompts/writing/
ruby bin/migrate_prompts ~/.prompts/code_review.txt ~/.prompts/debug_help.txt
AIA_PROMPTS__DIR=~/old-prompts ruby bin/migrate_prompts --dry-run
Option Effect --dry-run Report what would happen; change nothing. --verbose Show the keys, parameters and description found in each file. --force Overwrite an existing .md file. Without it, a .txt whose .md already exists is skipped. --reprocess Look at *.txt-review files again and migrate the ones that now pass. -h, --help Show usage.

The original .txt and .json files are left in place. Delete them yourself once you're happy with the .md versions.

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text:
Old New Parameter [TOPIC] <%= topic %> topic [FILE_NAME] <%= file_name %> file_name [TARGET AUDIENCE] <%= target_audience %> target_audience (spaces become underscores)

Each parameter's default is the most recent value from the .json history file, or null (ask every time) if there is none.

docs.title: Directives
docs.text:
Old line Becomes //config KEY VALUE or //config KEY=VALUE KEY: VALUE at the top level for model, temperature, top_p, next, pipeline, shell and erb; otherwise under config: (max_tokens → config: / llm: / max_tokens:). Dotted keys nest under config: as written. true/false and numbers keep their types. //temp 0.3 temperature: 0.3 //topp 0.9 top_p: 0.9 //next other_prompt next: other_prompt //pipeline a, b, c pipeline: [a, b, c] //include FILE <%= include('FILE') %> //shell COMMAND <%= `COMMAND` %>, which inserts the command's output //ruby CODE <%= CODE %>, with placeholders turned into parameter names //backend … Dropped. Any other //name … Left in the body unchanged, with an Unrecognized directive warning in the summary.

When a directive argument contains a placeholder, it becomes the parameter: //include [FILE] turns into <%= include(file) %>.

A placeholder in a //shell command becomes an interpolated parameter: //shell ls [DIR] turns into <%= `ls #{dir}` %>. See ERB & Shell.

docs.title: Everything else
docs.text: Old New #! shebang on line 1 Kept on line 1, above the front matter. # ~/.prompts/name.txt path comment Dropped. # Desc: … (and indented # continuation lines) description: in front matter. Other # comment lines HTML comments (<!-- … -->), which aia strips before sending the prompt. Text after __END__ One HTML comment at the end of the file. Multi-line <% … %> blocks Copied unchanged.

docs.title: Files flagged for review
docs.text:
The script won't guess when a file is ambiguous. It renames name.txt to name.txt-review and leaves it for you when the file:

  • contains a fenced code block (```), where a [NAME] might be code rather than a placeholder;
  • has a placeholder inside ERB (<%= [NAME] %>);
  • has bracketed text that looks like a placeholder attempt but isn't a clean one, such as [LANGUAGE code] or [e.g. JSON].

Bracketed text that clearly isn't a placeholder — shell tests like [ -z "$x" ], [ActiveRecord::Base], ["a", "b"], camelCase, or anything 50 characters or longer — doesn't cause a flag.

To deal with a flagged file, either:

  1. Fix it and reprocess. Edit the .txt-review file so its placeholders are clean [UPPER_CASE] names (or remove the brackets that aren't placeholders), then run the command below. A file with a fenced code block is flagged every time, so convert those by hand.

    ruby bin/migrate_prompts --reprocess --dry-run
ruby bin/migrate_prompts --reprocess

    Files that now pass are renamed back to .txt and migrated; the rest stay flagged.

  2. Convert it by hand into a new .md file using the format above, then delete the .txt-review.

docs.title: After migrating
docs.text:
1. Look over a few converted files, especially ones that had //shell, //ruby or Unrecognized directive warnings.
  2. Run a converted prompt: aia summarize report.md. aia asks for each parameter whose default is null.
  3. Remove the old .txt and .json files.

docs.title: Upgrading to 2.0
docs.text: aia 2.0 is a rebuild, not a drop-in replacement for 1.x. This page lists what changes for you between 1.1.1, the last 1.x release, and 2.0.0 — work through it before upgrading — followed by a short tour of what's new.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1.1.1 2.0.0 Ruby 3.2 or newer 4.0.9 or newer

Install or upgrade with:

gem install aia
aia --version     # 2.0.0

The ruby_llm-mcp gem is no longer used, and it cannot be loaded alongside the version of ruby_llm that aia 2.0 needs. If you have it in a --require list or a Gemfile next to aia, remove it.

docs.title: Removed command-line options
docs.text:
Passing one of these now stops aia with an error and exit status 1:

$ aia --terse my_prompt
ERROR: invalid option: --terse
       use --help for usage report
Removed option What to do instead --terse Nothing. It had no effect in 1.x. --regex PATTERN Nothing. Parameters are ERB (<%= name %>), so a custom placeholder pattern no longer means anything. --skills-prefix PREFIX Point --skills-dir at the directory that holds your skill subdirectories. --md, --[no-]markdown Nothing. Responses are written as the model returns them.

Check shell aliases, scripts, cron jobs and executable prompts' #! lines for these.

docs.title: Removed keys
docs.text:
These are ignored if they are still in your config file, as are their AIA_* environment variables. They don't appear in aia --dump either:

Removed key Notes flags.terse See --terse. prompts.parameter_regex See --regex. prompts.skills_prefix See --skills-prefix. output.markdown See --md. prompts.roles_dir, roles.dir Roles are always found in prompts.dir/prompts.roles_prefix. prompts.tool, prompts.tools_prefix, tools.dir Load tools with --tools or tools.paths. embedding.model Nothing used it. flags.clear Use the /clear directive. paths.config_file aia finds your config file in its standard place (~/.config/aia/aia.yml, or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/aia/aia.yml when that is set); use -c for another one.

docs.title: Changed defaults
docs.text:
If you relied on an old default, set it in your config file.

Key 1.1.1 default 2.0.0 default llm.max_tokens 2048 32767 llm.top_p 1.0 unset (the provider's default) audio.speak_command afplay say audio.voice alloy unset audio.speech_model tts-1 unset audio.transcription_model whisper-1 unset

afplay plays audio files, not text, so --speak didn't work with the old default. The old voice and audio-model defaults only made sense for OpenAI. To keep OpenAI text-to-speech, use a script as your speak command — see Images & Speech.

To restore the old response-length cap, for example:

llm:
  max_tokens: 2048

docs.title: Chat directives
docs.text:
• /terse is gone.
  • /ruby is off by default. It runs any Ruby with aia's full privileges. Start aia with --allow-ruby-eval to use it. See Security.
  • /model keeps the conversation. Switching models now hands the new model a summary of the conversation so far; in 1.x the new model started fresh. Set model_switch_history: clean to start fresh as 1.x did, or replay to re-send your messages. See Chat Sessions.

Every other 1.x directive and alias still works.

docs.title: Custom tools
docs.text:
Tool files loaded with --tools must use the ruby_llm 2 style of declaring parameters. param … desc: is now parameter … description::

# 1.x
param :text, desc: "Text to process"

# 2.0
parameter :text, description: "Text to process"

A tool still written the 1.x way fails with NoMethodError when aia loads it. See Tools.

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text:
Servers listed under mcp_servers: keep working, with three exceptions:

  • The sse and ws transports are gone. Use the server's Streamable HTTP endpoint (url:) or run it locally over stdio (command:). A server still set to sse or ws is reported as failed at startup.
  • Two servers can't offer a tool with the same name. The second one fails to connect. Give one of them a prefix: so its tool names are distinct.
  • Server classes loaded with --require must be RubyLLM::MCP subclasses, and they are no longer picked up automatically. List them by class name under mcp_servers: (see Naming a server class).

See MCP Servers.

docs.title: Files no longer in the gem
docs.text: The installed gem contains only what aia needs to run. The documentation, the examples/ directory, the mcp_servers/ samples and the bin/migrate_prompts script are in the GitHub repository only.

docs.title: If you used a 2.0 pre-release
docs.text:
These existed in the 2.0 alpha and beta releases and were removed before 2.0.0:

  • The KBS rule engine, the /rules directive, user-defined rule hooks and --tool-filter-kbs.

  • The zvec, sqlite-vec and LSI tool filters. TF-IDF is the only tool filter; it is on by default and switched with -A / --[no-]auto-tool-filter. This replaces the tool_filter_a setting.

  • --expert-routing (flags.expert_routing), --load and --save (flags.tool_filter_load, flags.tool_filter_save), concurrency.independent_servers, the MCP server key independent:, and switching models by typing "switch to claude". Passing one of these options is now an invalid-option error, and the keys are ignored. Use /model to switch models.

-A used to mean --tool-filter-kbs; it now means --auto-tool-filter.

docs.title: What's new in 2.0
docs.text:
A quick tour, with where to read more:

  • Any provider ruby_llm supports, local or hosted. --provider sets the default for model names without a prefix, --list-providers shows what's available, and --list-models asks a provider what it is serving. Choosing Models, Local Models
  • Crews. Every chat is a team of robots. Add members with /add_recruit, address them with @name or @crew, and spawn one-shot specialists with /spawn. Crews
  • Multi-robot modes: /verify, /debate, /decompose, /delegate, /orchestrate. Advanced Modes
  • Multi-model turns run in parallel, with --consensus to merge the answers. Multi-Model & Consensus
  • MCP: servers connect once, in parallel, and are shared by every robot; Streamable HTTP servers (url:); per-server prefix:, only:, except: and requires_approval:; and --tool-approval. MCP Servers, Security
  • /model mid-session, carrying the conversation over.
  • Skills with -s / --skill. Roles & Skills
  • --[no-]thinking hides or shows the <think> reasoning that some local models stream.
  • Speech: --speak-command, --speech-model, --transcription-model and --voice all take effect. Images & Speech
  • --history-file / --no-history-file control chat input history.

docs.title: Upgrade checklist
docs.text:
• Ruby 4.0.9 or newer: ruby -v
  • Remove --terse, --regex and --skills-prefix from scripts and aliases.
  • Remove flags.terse, prompts.parameter_regex and prompts.skills_prefix from your config file (optional; they are ignored).
  • Set llm.max_tokens or the audio.* keys if you relied on the old defaults.
  • Update custom tools from param … desc: to parameter … description:.
  • Switch MCP servers off sse / ws; add prefix: where two servers share a tool name.
  • Add --allow-ruby-eval where you really use /ruby.
  • Still on prompt_manager's old .txt + .json prompt format? See Migrating Prompts.
  • Run aia --dump /tmp/check.yml and look it over.

docs.title: The Config File
docs.text: Your personal configuration lives in one YAML file, ~/.config/aia/aia.yml. Anything you set there becomes your default for every run, so you stop retyping the same options.

docs.title: Where aia looks
docs.text:
aia does not create a config file for you. It uses the first of these that exists:

  1. $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/aia/aia.yml, if XDG_CONFIG_HOME is set
  2. ~/.config/aia/aia.yml
  3. ~/Library/Application Support/aia/aia.yml (macOS only)

It also reads ./config/aia.yml in the current directory, if there is one. That file sits on top of your personal one, so a project can carry its own model, prompts directory or MCP servers. See Configuration Precedence.

docs.title: Your first config file
docs.text:
Create the file with only the settings you want to change. Everything you leave out keeps its built-in default.

mkdir -p ~/.config/aia
$EDITOR ~/.config/aia/aia.yml

# ~/.config/aia/aia.yml
models:
  - name: claude-sonnet-4-6

llm:
  temperature: 0.5

output:
  file: false      # don't leave a temp.md behind after every run

Check that aia picked it up:

$ aia --dump /tmp/now.yml && grep -A3 '^models' /tmp/now.yml
Config successfully dumped to /tmp/now.yml
models:
- :name: claude-sonnet-4-6
  :role:
  :instance: 1

YAML gotchas

  • Indent with spaces, never tabs.
  • ~ on its own means null, and a null in your config file is ignored — the built-in default stays. To switch something off, use false. (~/notes is still a path in your home directory.)
  • Quote values that YAML would otherwise reinterpret, such as "yes", "no", "on" or "1.10".
  • If the file can't be parsed, aia carries on without it (printing a MywayConfig: Failed to parse XDG config warning, unless Ruby warnings are switched off), so a typo can quietly put you back on the defaults. Run aia --dump after editing.

docs.title: How the file is organized
docs.text:
The file uses the same sections as the built-in defaults. You can use as many or as few as you like:

Section What it controls models Which model or models answer. llm Temperature, max tokens and other generation parameters. prompts Where prompts and roles live; default role, skills and chat system prompt. skills Where skills live. output The response file, appending, chat input history. audio Speech: voice, speak command, speech and transcription models. image Image generation model, size, quality, style. tools Tool files to load, allow/reject lists, tool-call approval. flags On/off switches: chat, tokens, cost, speak, debug … logger Where the aia, LLM and MCP logs go and how detailed they are. mcp_servers MCP servers to connect to. concurrency Running MCP servers in parallel. paths aia's own directory and the plugins directory. require_libs Ruby libraries to load at startup.

Every key, with its type and default, is in Configuration Keys.

docs.title: Use a different model by default
docs.text:
models:
  - name: claude-haiku-4-5

Several entries run every prompt on every model:

models:
  - name: gpt-4o
  - name: claude-sonnet-4-6
flags:
  consensus: true     # merge their answers into one

docs.title: Run local models
docs.text:
models:
  - name: ollama/llama3.2

See Local Models.

docs.title: Keep prompts in a project or a synced folder
docs.text:
prompts:
  dir: ~/Dropbox/prompts
skills:
  dir: ~/Dropbox/prompts/skills

Roles move with prompts.dir (they live in its roles subdirectory), but skills.dir doesn't follow it automatically. Also export AIA_PROMPTS__DIR so shell completion finds the same place, since the completion scripts can't read the config file and otherwise look in ~/.prompts (see Environment Variables).

docs.title: Always show tokens and cost
docs.text:
flags:
  cost: true
  tokens: true

docs.title: Keep a running log of every answer
docs.text:
output:
  file: ~/notes/aia_answers.md
  append: true

docs.title: Load your tools every time
docs.text:
require_libs:
  - shared_tools
tools:
  paths:
    - ~/.config/aia/tools/weather_tool.rb
    - ~/.config/aia/tools/jira_tool.rb
  rejected:
    - delete

List individual .rb files under tools.paths; only --tools on the command line expands a directory. See Tools.

docs.title: Connect MCP servers
docs.text:
mcp_servers:
  - name: filesystem
    command: npx
    args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "~/projects"]

See MCP Servers for every server option.

docs.title: Quieter or louder logs
docs.text:
logger:
  aia:
    level: info
  llm:
    file: ~/.config/aia/logs/llm.log
    level: debug

docs.title: Alternate config files with -c
docs.text:
-c FILE (--config-file FILE) runs aia with a different config file instead of your personal one. Useful for switching between setups:

aia -c ~/.config/aia/local.yml --chat      # everything local
aia -c ~/.config/aia/work.yml standup      # work models and MCP servers

With -c, aia starts from its built-in defaults and applies only FILE and your command-line options. It ignores ~/.config/aia/aia.yml, ./config/aia.yml and the AIA_* environment variables — except AIA_MODEL and AIA_PLUGINS_DIR, which still apply. A missing file stops aia:

$ aia -c ~/.config/aia/wrok.yml standup
ERROR: Config file not found: /Users/you/.config/aia/wrok.yml

docs.title: See what aia is using
docs.text:
--dump FILE writes the complete, final configuration — defaults, files, environment and the other options on the same command line — and exits without running anything:

aia --dump /tmp/now.yml
aia -m gpt-4o -t 0.1 --dump /tmp/with_flags.yml   # include command-line options

The file must end in .yml or .yaml. Keys aia doesn't know (a typo, or a setting removed in 2.0) are dropped when the configuration loads, so they don't appear; if a setting you wrote is missing from the dump, check its spelling. In the output, keys inside each section are written with a leading colon (:temperature: 0.7); that is how YAML writes Ruby symbols and doesn't affect reading it.

Use --dump to debug settings, not to create your config file: it records every value, including paths already expanded and defaults you never chose, which then stop following future changes to aia's defaults.

Inside a chat session, /config shows the live configuration and /config KEY VALUE changes a setting for the rest of the session. See Directives.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: Environment variables let you set aia's options per shell, per project (with a tool like direnv) or per command, without touching a config file. They also carry your provider API keys.

docs.title: Setting any config key: AIA_*
docs.text:
Every key in the configuration can be set with an environment variable. Take the key's dotted path, write it in capitals, join the levels with __ (two underscores), and put AIA_ in front:

Config key Environment variable llm.temperature AIA_LLM__TEMPERATURE prompts.dir AIA_PROMPTS__DIR output.file AIA_OUTPUT__FILE flags.tokens AIA_FLAGS__TOKENS logger.llm.level AIA_LOGGER__LLM__LEVEL require_libs AIA_REQUIRE_LIBS

Configuration Keys lists the variable for every key.

# for one command
AIA_OUTPUT__FILE=dates.md aia extract_dates contract.txt

# for the rest of the shell session
export AIA_PROMPTS__DIR=~/work/prompts
export AIA_SKILLS__DIR=~/work/prompts/skills

Environment variables override your config file and are overridden by command-line options. See Configuration Precedence.

How values are read

Environment values are text, so aia converts each one to the type of the setting it controls:

  • On/off settings accept true, yes, on, 1 and false, no, off, 0 (any case): AIA_FLAGS__TOKENS=false.
  • Numbers are converted: AIA_LLM__TEMPERATURE=0.2, AIA_LLM__MAX_TOKENS=800.
  • Lists are split on commas: AIA_TOOLS__ALLOWED=read,write, AIA_TOOLS__PATHS=~/tools/a.rb,~/tools/b.rb, AIA_REQUIRE_LIBS=shared_tools,json.

A value that doesn't fit (for example AIA_LLM__MAX_TOKENS=lots) is kept as text, and the setting may then not work. Run aia --dump check.yml to see exactly what aia made of your variables.

docs.title: AIA_MODEL
docs.text:
The model or models to use, in the same form as -m:

export AIA_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5
export AIA_MODEL="gpt-4o,claude-sonnet-4-6"       # run both
export AIA_MODEL="gpt-4o=architect,gpt-4o=critic" # same model, two roles
export AIA_MODEL=ollama/llama3.2                  # provider prefix

-m on the command line wins over AIA_MODEL. AIA_MODEL also wins over the models: in a file given with -c.

docs.title: AIA_PLUGINS_DIR
docs.text:
The plugins directory (config key paths.plugins_dir). Note the name: it is AIA_PLUGINS_DIR, not AIA_PATHS__PLUGINS_DIR. --plugins-dir wins over it. Like AIA_MODEL, it still applies when you use -c. See Plugins.

export AIA_PLUGINS_DIR=~/.config/aia/plugins

docs.title: AIA_PROMPTS__DIR and AIA_PROMPTS__ROLES_PREFIX
docs.text: These set prompts.dir and prompts.roles_prefix like any other variable. AIA_PROMPTS__DIR matters in one more place: the shell completion scripts from aia --completion read it directly, because they run in your shell and can't read the config file. They fall back to ~/.prompts when it is unset. If you keep prompts somewhere other than ~/.prompts and want completion, export AIA_PROMPTS__DIR rather than setting prompts.dir only in the config file.

docs.title: AIA_SKILLS__DIR
docs.text: Sets skills.dir. Its default, ~/.prompts/skills, does not follow AIA_PROMPTS__DIR, so if you move your prompts and keep skills beside them, set both.

docs.title: Provider API keys
docs.text:
Keys use each provider's usual variable name. Set the ones for the providers you use:

Provider Variable(s) OpenAI OPENAI_API_KEY Anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Google Gemini GEMINI_API_KEY DeepSeek DEEPSEEK_API_KEY Mistral MISTRAL_API_KEY Perplexity PERPLEXITY_API_KEY OpenRouter OPENROUTER_API_KEY xAI XAI_API_KEY GPUStack GPUSTACK_API_KEY AWS Bedrock AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_REGION, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN Google Vertex AI GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT, GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION

The default model, gpt-4o-mini, needs OPENAI_API_KEY. Local providers such as Ollama and LM Studio need no key.

aia --list-providers marks each provider that has a key with (has API key); for that check aia looks for <PROVIDER>_API_KEY (for example COHERE_API_KEY).

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
aia -m claude-haiku-4-5 my_prompt

docs.title: Provider endpoints: <PROVIDER>_API_BASE
docs.text:
For any provider that has a configurable endpoint, <PROVIDER>_API_BASE points it somewhere else — a local server on a different port, a proxy, a self-hosted gateway. <PROVIDER> is the provider's slug from aia --list-providers, in capitals.

export OLLAMA_API_BASE=http://gpu-box.local:11434/v1
export OPENAI_API_BASE=https://llm-proxy.example.com/v1

See Local Models.

docs.title: Other variables aia reads
docs.text: Variable Used for PUREMD_API_KEY Required by the /webpage directive, which fetches pages through the pure.md service. XDG_CONFIG_HOME If set, aia looks for its config file at $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/aia/aia.yml first. See The Config File. COLUMNS Width used to wrap --list-tools output. BUNDLE_GEMFILE Only when running bin/aia from a clone of the aia repository.

docs.title: Variables aia sets for you
docs.text: When aia runs your speak command (--speak with --speak-command, or the /say directive) it passes the speech model as SPEECH_MODEL in that command's environment.

docs.title: Configuration Precedence
docs.text: A setting can come from several places at once. This page shows the order aia applies them in, so you can predict which value wins and track down a surprise.

docs.title: The layers
docs.text:
aia starts from its built-in defaults and applies each layer on top of the last. A later layer overrides only the keys it sets; everything else passes through.

# Layer Where it comes from 1 Built-in defaults Shipped with aia. Listed in Configuration Keys. 2 Personal config file ~/.config/aia/aia.yml (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/aia/aia.yml). See The Config File. 3 Project config file ./config/aia.yml in the directory you run aia from. 4 Environment variables AIA_*, such as AIA_LLM__TEMPERATURE, plus AIA_MODEL and AIA_PLUGINS_DIR. See Environment Variables. 5 Command-line options -m, -t, --chat … See Command-Line Options. 6 Prompt front matter The YAML at the top of a prompt file, applied when that prompt is loaded. See Prompt Files. 7 /config and friends Directives you type during a chat: /config, /model, /temperature, /top_p.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
Suppose every layer has an opinion about the temperature:

# ~/.config/aia/aia.yml                 (layer 2)
llm:
  temperature: 0.7

# ~/work/api/config/aia.yml             (layer 3)
llm:
  temperature: 0.4

<!-- ~/.prompts/extract_dates.md        (layer 6) -->
---
temperature: 0.0
---
List every date mentioned in the text, one per line, in ISO 8601.
You run (from ~/work/api) Temperature used Why aia --chat 0.4 The project file overrides your personal file. AIA_LLM__TEMPERATURE=0.9 aia --chat 0.9* The environment overrides both files. aia -t 0.2 --chat 0.2 The command line overrides the environment.

* aia converts the text 0.9 to a number; see Environment Variables. The order is the same for every key.

If you then run aia -t 0.2 extract_dates contract.txt, the prompt's temperature: 0.0 replaces 0.2 when the prompt is loaded, so that prompt runs at 0.0.

Check any combination without calling a model by adding --dump:

$ cd ~/work/api && aia -t 0.2 --dump /tmp/c.yml && grep temperature /tmp/c.yml
Config successfully dumped to /tmp/c.yml
  :temperature: 0.2

--dump shows layers 1–5. Front matter and directives are applied later, while aia runs.

docs.title: When layers 6 and 7 take effect
docs.text:
aia builds the model connection (the robot) once, at startup, from layers 1–5. Front matter and directives are applied later, while aia runs, and they update the configuration from that point on:

  • Model settings apply before the next prompt or chat turn. temperature:, top_p: and config: llm: in a prompt's front matter, and /temperature, /top_p or /config llm.… in chat, retune the running robot (and every crewmate) in place, so the conversation is kept.
  • A different model rebuilds the robot. A front-matter model: switches models before that prompt runs, the same way /model does in chat, and carries the conversation over as model_switch_history says (see Chat Sessions).
  • Other settings apply right away — for example the output file, the pipeline (next: / pipeline:), or flags such as tokens.

docs.title: Front matter lasts for the rest of the run
docs.text: When aia loads a prompt, its front matter changes the running configuration and the change stays in place. In a pipeline, a setting made by the first prompt is still in effect for the second prompt unless that prompt sets its own.

docs.title: -c replaces layers 2–4
docs.text:
-c FILE (--config-file) swaps in a different configuration instead of adding another layer. With it, aia applies:

  1. Built-in defaults
  2. FILE
  3. AIA_MODEL and AIA_PLUGINS_DIR, if set
  4. Command-line options
  5. Front matter and directives, as usual

Your personal config file, any ./config/aia.yml, and all other AIA_* variables are ignored for that run. Use it to keep self-contained setups — "local models only", "work account" — that your everyday settings can't leak into.

docs.title: Lists are replaced, not merged
docs.text:
When a higher layer sets a list — models, pipeline, tools.paths, mcp_servers — it replaces the lower layer's list. -m gpt-4o on the command line means only gpt-4o, even if your config file lists three models.

Some command-line options add to what came before them on the same command line: -m, -s, -n, -p, --rq, --at, --rt, --mu, --ms and --mcp can be repeated. --mcp FILE adds its servers to the mcp_servers from your config file.

docs.title: Troubleshooting a setting
docs.text:
1. Run aia --dump /tmp/c.yml with the same options and from the same directory. If the value is wrong there, it comes from layers 1–5.
  2. Run env | grep '^AIA_' to spot a forgotten export.
  3. Look for config/aia.yml in the current directory.
  4. If --dump looks right but the run doesn't, check the prompt's front matter: it is applied after --dump reads the configuration.
  5. In chat, /config shows the live values.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: aia runs with your user account's permissions. Prompt files can run shell commands and Ruby, tools can act on your system, and whatever you send goes to a model provider. This page shows where each of those happens and how to keep it under control.

docs.title: Protect your API keys
docs.text:
• Keep provider keys in environment variables (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY …), set in your shell profile or a secrets manager. aia has no config key for them, so they never need to be in aia.yml.
  • Never write a key into a prompt file. Prompts get shared, committed and pasted into chats.

  • MCP servers can carry credentials in your config file (bearer_token:, headers:, env:). If yours does, make the file private:

    chmod 600 ~/.config/aia/aia.yml

  • aia --dump FILE writes your whole configuration, MCP credentials included. Don't share a dump without reading it.

  • At debug level the LLM log records request details. Don't leave --debug or --log-to pointed at a shared location.

docs.title: What runs code
docs.text: Source What it can do Default How to control it $(command) and $VAR in a prompt file Runs the command; inserts environment variables On shell: false in the prompt's front matter ERB (<%= %>, <% %>) in a prompt file Runs any Ruby On erb: false in the prompt's front matter Text piped to aia with no prompt ID Treated as a prompt, so $(...) and ERB in it run On Give a prompt ID; piped text is then appended as plain context Executable prompts (#! files) Same as any prompt file — Read before running /ruby directive Runs any Ruby Off --allow-ruby-eval / flags.allow_ruby_eval --tools, --require, tools.paths, require_libs Loads Ruby code into aia Off Only load code you trust Plugins directory Loads every *.rb file in it, and reloads changes during chat Off Only put files you trust there Tools the model calls Whatever the tool does — --at / --rt MCP servers A local server is a program aia starts as you; a remote one is a service you connect to Off Configure only servers you trust; see below

docs.title: Shell expansion and ERB in prompts
docs.text:
Prompt files are processed before they are sent: $(command) is replaced by the command's output, $NAME / ${NAME} by the environment variable (upper-case names only), and ERB is evaluated as Ruby. That's what makes prompts dynamic — and it means opening a prompt file with aia is running it.

---
description: Summarize today's commits
---
Summarize these commits for a standup:

$(git log --since=midnight --oneline)

Text inside fenced code blocks (``` or ~~~) is left alone by shell expansion. Command output is never re-expanded, and it can't inject ERB.

If a prompt only needs plain text, switch processing off in its front matter:

---
shell: false
erb: false
---

To switch it off for every prompt, set flags.shell: false and flags.erb: false in your config file; a prompt's own shell: / erb: front matter still wins. See ERB & Shell.

Piped text with no prompt ID is a prompt

some_command | aia (with no prompt ID) runs the piped text as a prompt, so $(...) and ERB in it are executed. Don't pipe untrusted content — a web page, an email, a downloaded file — into aia without a prompt ID. With a prompt ID (some_command | aia summarize), piped text and context files are appended as plain text and nothing in them runs.

docs.title: /ruby
docs.text:
The /ruby (/rb) directive evaluates Ruby inside aia with full privileges. It is off unless you start aia with --allow-ruby-eval or set flags.allow_ruby_eval: true. When it is off, using it prints an error and does nothing. When it is on, aia prints WARNING: /ruby executing: … to stderr every time.

Enable it only for sessions where you need it, never in a shared config file.

docs.title: Tools, libraries and plugins
docs.text:
Files given to --tools, gems given to --require, and files in the plugins directory are Ruby code that runs inside aia when it starts. Treat them like any program you install.

Tools are called by the model, not by you. A tool that writes files or runs commands can do so whenever the model decides to. To limit what the model can reach:

aia --chat --rq shared_tools --at read,search      # only tools whose names contain these
aia --chat --rq shared_tools --rt delete,shell,exec # everything except these

Matching is by substring, case-insensitive. Run aia --list-tools (with the same options) to see what is left. Note that the automatic tool filter (-A) chooses tools by relevance; it is not a security boundary.

docs.title: Tool approval
docs.text:
Tools from an MCP server marked requires_approval: true don't run until they're approved. The same rule covers an MCP server asking you for input. tools.approval (--tool-approval) decides what happens:

Mode Behavior ask (default) aia shows the tool and its arguments and asks Allow it? [y/N]. Anything but yes refuses. With no terminal (in a script or cron job), the call is refused. approve Every such call runs without asking. deny Every such call is refused. 
mcp_servers:
  - name: github
    command: github-mcp-server
    args: ["stdio"]
    requires_approval: true
tools:
  approval: ask

Approval applies to every robot aia builds, including crew members and spawned specialists. It covers MCP servers marked requires_approval: and any tool whose author declared requires_approval in the tool itself. Other tools you load with --tools or --require run without asking, so restrict those with --at / --rt.

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text:
• A stdio server (command:) is a program aia launches with your permissions. Install servers from sources you trust and pin their versions.
  • A remote server (url:) receives your prompts' tool calls and whatever data they include.
  • Expose only the tools you need with the server's only: / except: lists, and mark servers that can change things requires_approval: true.
  • Use --mcp-use NAMES to connect only the servers a session needs, or --no-mcp to connect none.
  • aia --mcp-list --list-tools shows exactly what each server offers before you use it.

See MCP Servers.

docs.title: What leaves your machine
docs.text:
Everything in a request goes to the model provider: the prompt, roles and skills, context files, piped text, tool results and the conversation so far. If something must not leave your machine, use a local model.

A few directives send data to other services:

  • /webpage URL fetches the page through the pure.md service (and needs PUREMD_API_KEY).
  • /paste puts your clipboard into the prompt — check what's on it.

docs.title: What aia writes to disk
docs.text:
File Contents Control temp.md in the current directory Every response; in chat, your messages too -o FILE, --no-output, output.file: false ~/.prompts/_prompts.log Lines you type at the chat prompt --history-file FILE, --no-history-file Log files you configure Activity; requests at debug level logger.*, --log-to

If you discuss sensitive material, turn the output and history files off or point them somewhere private.

docs.title: A short checklist
docs.text:
• API keys only in environment variables; chmod 600 any config file that holds tokens.
  • Read a prompt file, executable prompt or plugin before running one you didn't write.
  • Don't pipe untrusted text into aia without a prompt ID.
  • Leave /ruby off unless you need it this session.
  • Restrict tools with --at / --rt; mark risky MCP servers requires_approval: true.
  • Use --tool-approval deny for unattended runs that shouldn't change anything.
  • Use a local model for data that must stay on your machine.

docs.title: Chat Sessions
docs.text: Chat mode turns AIA into an interactive conversation in your terminal. The model remembers everything said so far, and you can steer the session as you go with / directives: switch models, pull in files, save and restore checkpoints, and more.

docs.title: Starting a chat
docs.text:
aia --chat                              # an empty conversation
aia --chat code_review lib/order.rb     # run a prompt first, then keep talking
aia --chat notes.md todo.md             # no prompt: the files are your first message
git diff | aia --chat                   # no prompt: the piped text is your first message
aia --chat --role tutor --model claude-sonnet-4-5

When you start with a prompt ID (or a pipeline), AIA runs it as usual, prints the answer, and then drops you into the conversation with that exchange already in context.

docs.title: What you'll see
docs.text:
A chat opens with a banner showing the AIA version and the session's setup: the model(s), the libraries in use, how many tools are loaded, which MCP servers connected (or failed), and the crew of robots you can address with @name:

       ,      ,        AIA v2.0.0 is Online
       (\____/)
        (_oo_)         Models: gpt-4o-mini
         (O)              DB: refreshed 2026-10-30 at 09:12
       __|||__    \)    Libs: ruby_llm v2.1.1, robot_lab v0.5.1, ...
     [/ Tobor \]  /    Tools: none loaded
    / \_______/ \/       MCP: (none configured)
   ...                  Crew: @tobor

Then the conversation starts:

Entering interactive chat mode...
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Follow up (cntl-D or 'exit' to end) #=>
How do I reverse a linked list in Ruby?

AI:
   You can reverse a singly linked list iteratively by walking it once
   and flipping each node's `next` pointer...

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Follow up (cntl-D or 'exit' to end) #=>

Answers stream in as the model writes them. A spinner shows while AIA is waiting for the first words.

docs.title: Ending a chat
docs.text:
Any of these ends the session and prints Chat session ended.:

  • Type exit
  • Press Ctrl+D
  • Press Enter on an empty line
  • Press Ctrl+C

An empty line ends the chat

Pressing Enter without typing anything is the same as exit. If you hit it by accident, you'll need to start again (your input history is kept, see below).

docs.title: Typing input
docs.text:
Each message is a single line. Press Enter to send it. For anything longer than a line (code, a log, a document), don't type it in: use /include FILE, /insert FILE or /paste instead (see Directives in chat).

The input line supports the usual editing keys (arrows, Home, End, Ctrl+A, Ctrl+E). Press Up and Down to step back through what you typed earlier. AIA keeps your last 50 entries in its history file, so they're still there next session. See Output, History and Usage.

docs.title: Your input is processed like a prompt
docs.text:
Each line you type goes through the same processing as a prompt file before it is sent:

  • $(command) is replaced by the command's output, and $VAR / ${VAR} by environment variables
  • <%= ... %> ERB is evaluated
  • <!-- ... --> comments are removed
Follow up (cntl-D or 'exit' to end) #=>
Here is my git status, what should I commit first? $(git status --short)

This is handy, and it also means a stray $(...) in your text will run. See ERB and Shell Expansion.

docs.title: Directives in chat
docs.text:
A line that starts with / is a directive, a command for AIA rather than a message for the model. /help lists them all. If you type one AIA doesn't know, it tells you:

Unknown directive: /switch  (use /help to see available directives)

When a directive produces output (a file, a web page, your clipboard), AIA shows it and then sends it to the model with a short note saying which directive it came from, so the model can use it. Directives that change settings or only display information (/model, /config, /checkpoint, /help, /cost) are not sent to the model.

The directives you'll use most in chat:

Directive What it does /help List every directive and its aliases /model [NAME[,NAME…]] Show the current model, or switch to another (see below) /models [TERMS] (aliases /available_models, /am, /llms, …) Search available models /config [KEY [VALUE]] (alias /cfg) Show all settings, show one, or change one /temperature N (alias /temp), /top_p N (alias /topp) Change those settings /include FILE Add a file, rendered like a prompt /insert FILE (alias /read) Add a file's raw text /paste (alias /clipboard) Add the clipboard contents /webpage URL (aliases /web, /website) Add a web page as Markdown (needs PUREMD_API_KEY) /skills [TERMS], /skill NAME List skills, or add one to the conversation (Roles and Skills) /checkpoint, /restore, /clear, /review, /checkpoints Manage the conversation (see below) /tools [FILTER], /mcp, /robots, /plugins Show loaded tools, MCP servers, the active robots, loaded plugins /cost Print this session's token and cost figures as CSV /say TEXT Speak text aloud with your speak command (say by default) /ruby CODE (alias /rb) Run Ruby code (only when started with --allow-ruby-eval)

Every directive, with all arguments and aliases, is in the Directives reference. Directives can also be used inside prompt files; see Directives.

docs.title: Switching models mid-conversation
docs.text:
/model

shows what you're talking to. To switch:

/model claude-sonnet-4-5
/model gpt-4o,gemini-2.5-pro        # switch to several models at once

AIA rebuilds the session with the new model, and by default the conversation comes with you. How the conversation is carried over is set by model_switch_history in your config file (or AIA_MODEL_SWITCH_HISTORY):

Value What the new model gets summarize (default) The old model writes a summary of the conversation, and the new model starts from that summary. This costs one request for the summary, plus one request per new model to hand it over. replay Every message you sent is re-sent to the new model, one at a time. The most faithful option, but one request per message you typed, per new model. clean Nothing. The new model starts fresh. 
model_switch_history: replay

/model also accepts short aliases such as sonnet, haiku, gpt4o, cheap or fast, and any you define under model_aliases in your config file:

model_aliases:
  writer: claude-sonnet-4-5

Only an exact alias is replaced, so a full model name is never changed.

When a switch carries history over, AIA tells you: Switching to claude-sonnet-4-5 (conversation: summarize)...

docs.title: Checkpoints: undo for conversations
docs.text:
Checkpoints let you save the conversation at a point and come back to it, which is useful for exploring a "what if" without polluting the main thread.

/checkpoint before_refactor
Checkpoint 'before_refactor' created at position 6.

...try an approach, decide you don't like it...

/restore before_refactor
Context restored to checkpoint 'before_refactor' (position 6).
Directive Effect /checkpoint [NAME] (aliases /ckp, /cp) Save the conversation. Without a name, checkpoints are numbered 1, 2, … /restore [NAME] Go back to a checkpoint. Without a name, goes back to the second most recent checkpoint (you need at least two). Checkpoints made after that point are discarded. /checkpoints (alias /checkpoints_list) List your checkpoints /review (alias /context) Show the conversation so far, with checkpoint markers /clear Forget the conversation but keep the system prompt (role, skills). Also deletes all checkpoints /clear --all Forget everything, including the system prompt and checkpoints

Checkpoints live in memory only. They disappear when the chat ends.

docs.title: Roles, skills and system prompts in chat
docs.text:
In chat, a --role and any --skills go into the system prompt, so they shape every answer rather than just the first one. You can also supply system prompt text directly:

aia --chat --system-prompt "Answer in British English. Be concise."

To bring a skill in partway through a conversation, use /skill NAME. See Roles and Skills.

docs.title: Talking to more than one model
docs.text:
Start a chat with several models and each one answers every message:

aia --chat --model gpt-4o,claude-sonnet-4-5

Each model runs as a named robot. Begin a message with @name to talk to just one of them, or @crew to address all of them explicitly:

@tobor what do you think of the other answer?

Use /robots to see the names. Building and managing a crew of robots, including adding and removing members during a chat, is covered in Crews. Merging the answers into one with --consensus is covered in Multiple Models and Consensus.

docs.title: Special modes for the next message
docs.text: A few directives change how AIA handles only your next message: /verify gets two independent answers and reconciles them, /decompose splits a task into parallel sub-tasks, /debate has the robots argue it out, and there are others (/concurrent, /delegate, /spawn, /orchestrate). Only one can be active at a time. They're explained in Advanced Modes.

docs.title: Other useful options for chat
docs.text:
Option Effect in chat --tokens / --cost Show token use, time (and cost) after every answer --speak Read every answer aloud (Images and Speech) --thinking Show <think>…</think> reasoning that some local models emit (hidden by default) --output FILE Record the conversation (your messages as You:, answers as AI:) --tools, --mcp Give the model tools and MCP servers

If you use plugins, AIA watches your plugins directory during a chat and loads, reloads or unloads plugin files as you add, edit or delete them, with no restart needed.

docs.title: Context Files and Piping
docs.text: Most useful prompts are about something: a file, a diff, a log, a web page. This chapter shows how to hand that material to AIA, and how to send AIA's answers on to other programs.

docs.title: Context files
docs.text:
Every file you list after the prompt ID is read and appended to the prompt, in the order you list them:

aia code_review app/models/order.rb app/models/line_item.rb

Your shell expands wildcards before AIA sees them, so globs work:

aia summarize notes/2026-10-*.md
aia code_review lib/**/*.rb        # zsh, or bash with `shopt -s globstar`

Things to know:

  • Files must exist. A missing file stops AIA before the model is called: The following files do not exist: …
  • Files are read as text and pasted in as-is. AIA does not send images, PDFs or other binary files as attachments. Convert them to text first (for example with pdftotext).
  • There is no size check. A large file is sent in full and counts against the model's context window and your token bill. Use --tokens to see how big a request was.
  • You need a prompt ID or --chat. Context files on their own give AIA nothing to ask. With --chat and no prompt, the files become your first chat message.

docs.title: Piping text in
docs.text:
Anything you pipe into AIA is added to the prompt:

git diff --staged | aia commit_msg
kubectl logs api-7f9c --since=1h | aia find_errors
curl -s https://api.example.com/status | aia explain_json

With no prompt ID, the piped text is the prompt:

echo "Write a haiku about merge conflicts." | aia
pbpaste | aia --chat          # macOS: start a chat about whatever's on the clipboard

If the piped text starts with a #! line, that line is dropped before the text is used.

You can combine stdin and context files. The prompt comes first, then stdin, then the files:

git diff main | aia code_review CONTRIBUTING.md

docs.title: Pulling content in from inside a prompt
docs.text:
Instead of passing material on the command line, a prompt file can fetch it itself:

In a prompt file What it does $(git log --oneline -20) Replaced with the command's output $HOME, ${PROJECT} Replaced with an environment variable (uppercase names only) <%= include 'includes/style.md' %> Inserts another prompt file, rendered <%= insert 'data/schema.sql' %> Inserts a file's raw text, untouched

These are covered in ERB and Shell Expansion and Directives.

docs.title: Adding content during a chat
docs.text:
In a chat session you can pull material in with directives:

Directive What it adds /include path/to/file.md A file, rendered like a prompt /insert path/to/file (alias /read) A file's raw text /paste (alias /clipboard) Whatever is on your system clipboard /webpage URL (aliases /web, /website) A web page converted to Markdown

AIA shows you the directive's output and then sends it to the model with a note saying which directive produced it.

/webpage needs a pure.md key

Web pages are fetched through the pure.md service, which turns them into clean Markdown. Set PUREMD_API_KEY in your environment to use it. Without it you'll see ERROR: PUREMD_API_KEY is required in order to include a webpage.

docs.title: Piping AIA's answer onward
docs.text:
AIA prints the answer to standard output, so you can pipe or redirect it:

aia release_notes CHANGELOG.md > release_notes.txt
aia summarize report.txt | pbcopy

The terminal output is meant for reading: it starts with an AI: label, shows the name of the robot that answered, and indents every line. The progress spinner goes to stderr, so it won't end up in your file.

For a file without the indentation, use AIA's output file instead. It gets each response as plain Markdown after an AI: label:

aia --output release_notes.md release_notes CHANGELOG.md

See Output, History and Usage.

docs.title: Patterns worth stealing
docs.text:
Review only what changed

git diff main...HEAD | aia code_review

Explain an error you just hit

bundle exec rake test 2>&1 | tail -50 | aia explain_failure

Summarize a directory of notes and keep talking

aia --chat summarize meetings/*.md

Ask a question about a command's output, no prompt file needed

{ echo "Which of these processes is using the most memory, and is that normal?"; ps aux | sort -nrk 4 | head -15; } | aia

docs.title: Choosing Models
docs.text: AIA can talk to any model that RubyLLM supports: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Mistral, OpenRouter, xAI, AWS Bedrock, local servers and more. This chapter shows how to pick a model, find the exact name to use, and tune how it answers.

docs.title: The default
docs.text: Unless you say otherwise, AIA uses gpt-4o-mini from OpenAI, which needs OPENAI_API_KEY. To use something else, choose one of the methods below.

docs.title: Choosing a model
docs.text:
For one runFor your shell sessionPermanentlyMid-chat 
aia --model claude-sonnet-4-5 summarize report.txt
aia -m gemini-2.5-flash --chat

export AIA_MODEL=claude-sonnet-4-5

AIA_MODEL takes a comma-separated list, just like --model.

# ~/.config/aia/aia.yml
models:
  - name: claude-sonnet-4-5

/model claude-sonnet-4-5

See Chat Sessions.

An option on the command line beats AIA_MODEL, which beats the config file. The full order is in Precedence.

docs.title: Model names
docs.text:
There are two ways to write a model name.

A catalog ID such as gpt-4o, claude-sonnet-4-5 or gemini-2.5-flash. RubyLLM knows which provider serves it.

provider/model such as ollama/llama3.2, openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 or gpustack/qwen3. Use this form for local servers and for gateways that serve other companies' models. AIA treats the part before the first / as a provider only if it is a registered provider (see --list-providers). Otherwise the whole string is used as the model name, which is why catalog IDs like meta-llama/llama-4-maverick still work.

If most of your models come from one provider, set it once with --provider and leave the prefix off:

aia --provider ollama -m llama3.2 --chat        # same as -m ollama/llama3.2

If AIA can't find the model you asked for, it stops before running anything:

<RubyLLM's "model not found" message>
Requested model(s): claude-sonet-4-5
Run 'aia --available-models' to see available models.

docs.title: Search the catalog: --available-models
docs.text:
RubyLLM ships a catalog of known models. Search it with --available-models, giving a comma-separated list of terms that must all match:

aia --available-models                     # everything
aia --available-models claude              # names/providers containing "claude"
aia --available-models openai,mini         # both terms

Available LLMs for openai and mini:

- gpt-4.1-mini (openai) text,image,pdf to text
- gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 (openai) text,image,pdf to text
- gpt-4o-mini (openai) text,image,pdf to text
...

53 LLMs matching your query

Each line shows the model ID, its provider, and what goes in and comes out. Terms are matched as plain text against the whole line (case matters), so a provider name such as anthropic or an input type such as pdf works as a filter too.

docs.title: Filter by capability
docs.text:
A term of the form INPUT_to_OUTPUT matches models by what they accept and produce, rather than by text: text_to_image finds models that take text and return images, audio_to_text finds transcription models, and so on. Combine it with other terms:

aia --available-models text_to_image,openai

docs.title: Ask a provider what it serves: --list-models
docs.text:
The catalog doesn't know about models on your own Ollama or LM Studio server, or brand-new ones. Ask the provider directly:

aia --provider ollama --list-models

ollama models:
------------------------------------------------------------
- ollama/llama3.2
- ollama/qwen3:8b

2 ollama model(s) available

--list-models needs --provider. Without it you'll get ERROR: --list-models requires --provider SLUG (use --available-models to search the full model registry).

docs.title: See which providers you can use: --list-providers
docs.text:
aia --list-providers

lists every registered provider, marking local ones with (local) and ones with a key in your environment with (has API key). Provider gems you load with --require show up too.

docs.title: Searching from inside a chat
docs.text:
/models claude
/models gpt -mini          # "gpt" but not "mini"

If your current model has a provider prefix (for example ollama/…), /models asks that provider for its live list. Otherwise it searches the catalog. Exclude terms with -, ~ or !.

docs.title: Tuning the answers
docs.text:
Option Config key Default What it does -t, --temperature N llm.temperature 0.7 Higher is more varied and creative, lower is more focused and repeatable --max-tokens N llm.max_tokens 32767 The most the model may write in one answer --top-p N llm.top_p (unset) Nucleus sampling. Leave unset unless you know you need it: some models reject requests that set both temperature and top-p --frequency-penalty N llm.frequency_penalty 0.0 Discourages repeating the same words --presence-penalty N llm.presence_penalty 0.0 Encourages moving on to new topics 
aia -t 0.2 extract_fields invoice.txt         # precise
aia -t 1.0 brainstorm                         # loose

AIA leaves out settings a model doesn't accept. For example, temperature isn't sent to models that don't support it, and the default max_tokens isn't sent at all when the model is named with a provider (ollama/llama3.2, or --provider), because local servers' context windows are small. That applies to gateway prefixes such as openrouter/… too; give --max-tokens a value other than 32767 if you want a cap sent.

docs.title: Using more than one model
docs.text:
Give --model a comma-separated list and every model answers in parallel:

aia -m gpt-4o,claude-sonnet-4-5,gemini-2.5-flash explain_code lib/parser.rb
aia -m gpt-4o,claude-sonnet-4-5 --consensus explain_code lib/parser.rb

Each model can have its own role (-m gpt-4o=optimist,claude-sonnet-4-5=skeptic), and the same model can appear more than once. How the answers are shown, compared and combined is covered in Multiple Models and Consensus.

docs.title: Local models
docs.text:
Models running on your own machine through Ollama, LM Studio or GPUStack need no API key and send nothing off your machine. Use the provider/model form:

aia -m ollama/llama3.2 --chat

Setup, endpoints and tips are in Local Models.

docs.title: Output, History and Usage
docs.text: Where AIA's answers go, what it remembers between sessions, how to see token counts and costs, and how to turn on logging when something goes wrong.

docs.title: The output file
docs.text:
Besides printing each answer, AIA appends it to an output file. Out of the box that file is temp.md in your current directory.

  • At the start of each run, AIA empties the output file (unless you ask it to append, below).
  • Each answer is written after an AI: label. In chat mode, each of your messages is written too, after You:, so the file becomes a transcript.
  • Token and cost tables from --tokens / --cost, and the CSV from /cost, are written there as well.
temp.md after a short chat
AI: **Tobor** (2.4s):
Here's a summary of the report...

You: Which section has the most risk?

AI: Section 4, the vendor migration...

docs.title: Choosing where output goes
docs.text:
You want… Do this A specific file --output notes/answer.md (-o). Relative paths are relative to where you run AIA. The default temp.md -o with no file name. Put it last or before another option: aia -o summarize notes.txt takes summarize as the output file name No output file at all --no-output To add to the file instead of replacing it --append (-a); --no-append to switch it back off No output file, ever output.file: ~ in your config file To always append output.append: true in your config file 
# ~/.config/aia/aia.yml
output:
  file: ~          # stop writing ./temp.md

Keep a running journal

aia --chat -a -o ~/journal/ai.md appends every chat to the same file, giving you a searchable log of everything you've asked.

When you generate an image with --paint, the image is saved next to the output file with a .png extension (temp.md becomes temp.png).

docs.title: Chat input history
docs.text:
AIA remembers the lines you type in chat, so Up and Down bring back earlier messages, even from previous sessions. It keeps the last 50 entries.

Setting Default output.history_file ~/.prompts/_prompts.log 
aia --chat --history-file ~/.config/aia/work_history    # use another file
aia --chat --no-history-file                            # don't save input history

If the history file grows beyond 10 MB, AIA renames it to <file>.1 at the start of a session and starts a fresh one, printing History log rotated: ….

Note

The history file holds what you typed, not the model's answers. For a record of the whole conversation, use the output file.

docs.title: Token counts and time: --tokens
docs.text:
aia --tokens summarize report.txt

After each answer AIA shows how many tokens went in and came out, and how long the answer took:

┌─────────────┬───────┬────────┬───────┬──────┐
│ Model       │ Input │ Output │ Total │ Time │
├─────────────┼───────┼────────┼───────┼──────┤
│ gpt-4o-mini │  1843 │    212 │  2055 │ 2.3s │
└─────────────┴───────┴────────┴───────┴──────┘

That compact table is what you see after each chat turn. When you run a prompt without --chat, the same figures appear under a Multi-Model Token Usage heading with a TOTAL row, even for one model, because one-shot runs go through AIA's robot network.

Input tokens include everything sent: the role, the prompt, skills, piped text, context files and, in chat, the conversation so far. If a request is bigger than you expected, this is where you'll see it.

docs.title: Cost: --cost
docs.text:
--cost does everything --tokens does and adds what the answer cost, plus what 1,000 answers like it would cost:

┌─────────────┬───────┬────────┬───────┬──────────┬───────┬──────┐
│ Model       │ Input │ Output │ Total │ Cost     │ x1000 │ Time │
├─────────────┼───────┼────────┼───────┼──────────┼───────┼──────┤
│ gpt-4o-mini │  1843 │    212 │  2055 │ $0.00040 │ $0.40 │ 2.3s │
└─────────────┴───────┴────────┴───────┴──────────┴───────┴──────┘

Prices come from the RubyLLM model catalog. When a model has no price listed (local models, very new models), the cost shows N/A.

With several models, you get one row per model under a Multi-Model Token Usage heading, plus a TOTAL row. Time in the total row is the slowest model's, because the models run in parallel.

docs.title: A whole session as CSV: /cost
docs.text: In a chat, /cost prints one CSV row per turn so far, plus a totals row, with the columns model,input_tokens,output_tokens,total_tokens,cost,elapsed. The CSV is also appended to the output file, so it's easy to pull into a spreadsheet.

docs.title: Logging and debugging
docs.text:
AIA has three logs:

Log Records aia AIA's own activity, including the full configuration at startup (at debug level) llm Requests to and responses from model providers mcp Connections to MCP servers

By default all three go to standard output and only show warnings and errors.

Option Effect --log-level LEVEL Set every log to debug, info, warn, error or fatal -d, --debug Shortcut for --log-level debug --no-debug Turn debug off again (handy when your config file turns it on) --log-to FILE Send all three logs to FILE instead of the terminal -v, --verbose Show extra detail, such as which tools were picked for each chat turn 
aia --debug --log-to /tmp/aia.log summarize report.txt
tail -f /tmp/aia.log            # in another terminal

Log files roll over daily. To set each log separately, use the logger section of the config file:

# ~/.config/aia/aia.yml
logger:
  aia:
    file: ~/.config/aia/logs/aia.log
    level: info
  llm:
    file: ~/.config/aia/logs/llm.log
    level: debug
  mcp:
    file: STDERR
    level: warn

file can be a path, STDOUT or STDERR. --log-level and --log-to override these settings for one run. In a chat you can change log levels on the fly with /config, for example /config logger.llm.level debug.

docs.title: Saving your settings
docs.text:
--dump FILE writes the configuration AIA would use (after your config file, environment variables and command-line options are combined) to a YAML file, then exits:

aia --model claude-sonnet-4-5 -t 0.3 --dump current.yml

That's a quick way to check what a combination of settings resolves to, or to start a new config file. The file must end in .yml or .yaml. See Config File.

docs.title: Roles and Skills
docs.text: Roles and skills are reusable blocks of instructions that you add to a prompt from the command line. A role says who the model should be ("a senior security reviewer"). A skill says how to do something ("our changelog format", "how to write a migration"). Keep them in files, and any prompt can use them.

docs.title: Creating a role
docs.text:
A role is a Markdown file in the roles folder of your prompts directory:

~/.prompts/roles/reviewer.md
You are a meticulous senior code reviewer.
Report bugs and security problems first, then readability, then style.
Quote the exact line you're commenting on.

The role ID is the path inside roles/ without .md. Subfolders work: ~/.prompts/roles/lang/ruby_expert.md is lang/ruby_expert.

docs.title: Using a role
docs.text:
aia --role reviewer code_review lib/payment.rb
aia -r lang/ruby_expert --chat

You can also give a path to a role file anywhere on disk. Start it with /, ./, ../ or ~/:

aia --role ./project_roles/onboarding_buddy.md explain setup.md
aia --role ~/team/roles/architect explain design.md     # .md is optional

What happens to the role depends on the mode:

Mode Where the role goes Running a prompt or pipeline Placed in front of each prompt's text, and also added to the system prompt --chat Added to the system prompt, so it applies to every turn (if you start the chat with a prompt ID, it is also placed in front of that prompt) --role with no prompt ID and no --chat The role file itself runs as the prompt

Both copies are processed like a prompt file: the front matter is removed, and ERB and $(...) are expanded. Roles given as a path work the same way as roles from the roles folder, in every mode.

docs.title: Listing roles
docs.text:
aia --list-roles

prints each role with a table of its front matter (if it has any), so a description: in a role's front matter makes the list more useful:

~/.prompts/roles/reviewer.md
---
description: Strict code reviewer, bugs first
---
You are a meticulous senior code reviewer. ...

Files and folders whose names start with _ are left out of the list, which is a convenient way to hide drafts.

docs.title: A different role per model
docs.text:
When you run several models at once, each can play its own role. Append =ROLE to the model name:

aia --model gpt-4o=optimist,claude-sonnet-4-5=skeptic --chat

AIA checks that each role file exists before starting. If one doesn't, it lists the roles it found. More in Multiple Models and Consensus.

docs.title: Changing the roles folder name
docs.text: The folder is called roles by default. To use a different subfolder of your prompts directory, pass --roles-prefix NAME or set prompts.roles_prefix in the config file.

docs.title: What a skill looks like
docs.text:
A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file. That's the same layout Claude Code uses for its skills, so you can share skills between the two.

~/.prompts/skills/
├── changelog/
│   └── SKILL.md
└── rails-migrations/
    └── SKILL.md
~/.prompts/skills/changelog/SKILL.md
---
name: changelog
description: Write CHANGELOG entries in our Keep a Changelog style
---
When writing a changelog entry:
- Group changes under Added, Changed, Fixed, Removed.
- One line per change, starting with a verb.
- Link the PR number at the end of the line.

The front matter describes the skill for listings. Only the text after it is added to your prompt.

docs.title: Using skills
docs.text:
aia --skill changelog release_notes CHANGELOG.md
aia -s changelog,rails-migrations --chat
aia -s changelog -s house-style summarize notes.md      # repeatable

You don't have to type the whole name. If there's no folder with exactly that name, AIA uses the first folder (alphabetically) whose name starts with what you typed, so -s rails finds rails-migrations.

A path works too, either to a skill folder (AIA reads its SKILL.md) or straight to a Markdown file. A file must end in .md or .markdown; any other file is refused with Warning: Skill '…' is not a markdown file:

aia -s ./skills/release-checklist --chat
aia -s ~/notes/house_style.md summarize report.txt

If a skill can't be found, AIA prints a warning (Warning: Skill 'x' not found in …) and carries on without it.

If your skills directory (see Where skills live) doesn't exist, each named skill is skipped with a warning. Skills given as a path still load.

Mode Where skills go Running a prompt or pipeline Appended after each prompt's text --chat Added to the system prompt

docs.title: Where skills live
docs.text:
AIA looks for skills in ~/.prompts/skills by default. That location doesn't follow --prompts-dir or AIA_PROMPTS__DIR. To use another folder:

aia --skills-dir ~/.claude/skills -s pdf --chat      # for one run
export AIA_SKILLS__DIR=~/.claude/skills              # for every run

or set skills.dir in your config file.

docs.title: Finding skills
docs.text:
From the command line:

aia --list-skills

lists every skill folder that has a SKILL.md, with a table of its front matter.

Inside a chat, /skills lists skills with their name and description, and takes search terms that are matched against each skill's front matter (case doesn't matter):

/skills                   # everything
/skills rails             # skills mentioning "rails"
/skills test -rspec       # mentioning "test" but not "rspec"

Prefix a term with -, ~ or ! to exclude it. A leading + is allowed for terms you want to require.

docs.title: Adding a skill partway through a chat
docs.text:
/skill changelog

adds that skill's SKILL.md to the conversation. Name matching works the same way as --skill.

docs.title: Roles or skills or prompts?
docs.text: Use a… When the text is… Example Role A persona or point of view that suits many tasks "You are a patient Ruby tutor" Skill Know-how for one kind of task, useful across prompts "How we write database migrations" Prompt The task itself "Review this pull request" Include A shared fragment inside specific prompt files A house style guide included by several prompts
