docs.title: Running Prompts
docs.text: This chapter covers every way to tell AIA what to send: a saved prompt, text on stdin, a fuzzy search, an executable prompt file, or nothing at all (straight into chat). It also explains how AIA builds the final text that the model sees.

docs.title: The command line in one picture
docs.text:
aia [options] [PROMPT_ID] [CONTEXT_FILE]*
aia [options] --chat [PROMPT_ID] [CONTEXT_FILE]*
  • Options start with - or -- and can go anywhere on the line.
  • PROMPT_ID names a prompt file in your prompts directory.
  • **CONTEXT_FILE**s are files whose contents are appended to the prompt.

docs.title: Running a saved prompt
docs.text:
A prompt ID is the name of a prompt file in your prompts directory without the .md extension:

File Prompt ID ~/.prompts/summarize.md summarize ~/.prompts/code_review.md code_review 
aia summarize report.txt
aia code_review lib/*.rb

Prompt files can live in subfolders, and their names can contain hyphens. ~/.prompts/dev/code-review.md has the ID dev/code-review. You can also name a prompt file by its path, starting with /, ./, ../ or ~/, such as aia ./drafts/idea.md.

Use a different prompts directory for one run with --prompts-dir DIR, or permanently with AIA_PROMPTS__DIR or prompts.dir in the config file.

docs.title: How AIA decides what's a prompt ID
docs.text:
AIA treats the first argument as a prompt ID only when both of these are true:

  1. It is not the name of an existing file in the current directory, and
  2. <prompts dir>/<argument>.md exists.

Otherwise the first argument is treated as a context file like the rest. So if you have a file called summarize in your working directory, aia summarize notes.txt will treat both as context files (and, with no prompt ID, stop with A prompt ID is required…). Rename the file or run from another directory.

If the first argument has no extension and is neither a prompt nor a file, AIA reports it as a missing prompt and suggests close matches. Here the prompt is code_review but a hyphen was typed:

No prompt named 'code-review' in /Users/you/.prompts (and no file by that name).
Did you mean: code_review?

Every other argument must be an existing file. If one isn't, AIA stops before calling the model:

The following files do not exist: notes.txt

docs.title: Asking without a prompt file
docs.text:
When you give no prompt ID, whatever you pipe in becomes the prompt:

echo "Suggest five names for a Ruby gem that parses invoices." | aia
git diff | aia            # the diff itself is the prompt
aia < question.txt

When you do give a prompt ID, piped text is appended to that prompt instead:

git diff --staged | aia commit_msg

See Context Files and Piping for more patterns.

Interactive input still works after a pipe

After reading stdin, AIA reconnects to your terminal, so a piped prompt can still ask you for parameter values, and --chat still works.

docs.title: Picking a prompt with fuzzy search
docs.text:
If fzf is installed, --fuzzy (-f) opens a searchable list of your prompts with a preview of each:

aia --fuzzy
aia -f --chat           # pick a prompt, then keep chatting

Press Esc to cancel.

docs.title: Running a prompt file directly
docs.text:
If the first file on the command line starts with a #! line, AIA treats that file as the prompt itself (the #! line is dropped). That is what makes executable prompts work:

aia ./weekly_report.md        # first line is #!/usr/bin/env aia ...
./weekly_report.md            # same thing, after chmod +x

docs.title: Chat with no prompt
docs.text:
--chat on its own starts an empty conversation:

aia --chat
aia --chat design_notes.md    # context files become your first message

See Chat Sessions.

docs.title: Running several prompts in a row
docs.text:
Use --pipeline (-p) or --next (-n) to run more than one prompt, each building on the last. Give the first prompt ID on the command line as usual; outside --chat, --pipeline on its own stops with A prompt ID is required…:

aia extract --pipeline summarize,translate report.txt
aia extract --next summarize report.txt

Pipelines are covered in Pipelines.

docs.title: What the model actually receives
docs.text:
For each prompt, AIA assembles the text in this order:

  1. The role, if you gave --role (see Roles and Skills)
  2. The prompt itself, after its parameters, shell references and ERB are filled in
  3. Any skills you gave with --skill
  4. Anything piped in on stdin
  5. The contents of each context file, in the order you listed them

Each part is separated by a blank line. In chat mode the skills go into the system prompt instead, so they apply to every turn. A role from your roles folder also goes into the system prompt, in every mode (see Roles and Skills).

A role on its own

aia --role editor with no prompt ID and no --chat runs the role file itself as the prompt. Add a prompt ID (aia --role editor tighten draft.md) to use the role as the system prompt for that prompt instead.

docs.title: Changing settings for one run
docs.text:
Most configuration can be overridden with an option. The ones you'll reach for most:

Option Effect -m, --model MODEL Which model to use (Choosing Models) -t, --temperature N Randomness of the answer (default 0.7) --max-tokens N Cap the length of the answer (default 32767) -r, --role ROLE Prepend a role -s, --skill IDS Append skills -o, --output [FILE] / --no-output Where to save the answer (Output, History and Usage) -c, --config-file FILE Use FILE instead of ~/.config/aia/aia.yml; it also replaces your AIA_* environment variables (except AIA_MODEL and AIA_PLUGINS_DIR) --tokens / --cost Show usage after each answer

The complete list is in the CLI reference; how options, environment variables and config files combine is explained in Precedence.

docs.title: Commands that just answer a question and exit
docs.text:
These don't call a model. They print information and quit:

Command Shows aia --help All options aia --version The installed version aia --available-models [QUERY] Models in the catalog (Choosing Models) aia --list-providers Registered providers and which have API keys aia --provider SLUG --list-models The live models a provider serves aia --list-roles Your role files and their front matter aia --list-skills Your skills aia --list-tools Loaded tools (add --mcp-list to include MCP server tools) aia --mcp-list Configured MCP servers aia --dump FILE.yml Writes your effective configuration to a YAML file aia --completion bash\|zsh\|fish A shell completion script

docs.title: Stopping AIA
docs.text: Press Ctrl+C to interrupt AIA at any time. It prints Interrupted. Exiting... and exits with status 130. Configuration errors (a missing prompt, a bad file name, an unknown option) exit with status 1 and a message on stderr, so AIA behaves well in scripts.

docs.title: Common messages
docs.text: Message Meaning A prompt ID is required unless you use --chat, --fuzzy, --pipeline or --role, … You ran aia with nothing to send. Context files alone aren't a prompt: add a prompt ID, --chat, or piped text. Error: Prompt ID 'x' does not exist at … A prompt named in --pipeline/--next isn't in your prompts directory. No prompt named 'x' in … (and no file by that name). The prompt ID is misspelled, or the prompt is in another directory. AIA suggests close matches. The following files do not exist: … A context file name is wrong. Unknown argument(s): _x … Did you mean: -x? You typed _ instead of - in front of an option.

docs.title: Advanced Modes
docs.text: In a chat, a few directives change how AIA handles your next message: double-checking an answer, splitting a big question into parts, letting robots debate, handing work to specialists, or running a full multi-robot build. This page covers each of them, plus AIA's task tracking with TrakFlow.

docs.title: How the modes work
docs.text:
Type the directive on its own line, then send your message:

> /verify
Verification mode enabled for next prompt.
> Is it safe to call fork() in a multithreaded program?
  • Each mode applies to one message and then switches off.
  • Only one mode can be set at a time. A second mode directive replaces the first.
  • These modes work only in chat sessions (--chat).
  • If a mode can't run, AIA handles the message normally. Some modes say so first; others, such as /debate with fewer than two robots or /concurrent with fewer than two server groups, just answer normally. If a mode fails part-way, AIA prints ... failed: <reason>. Falling back to normal mode.
Directive Alias What happens to the next message /verify Two independent answers, then a reconciled one /decompose Split into sub-tasks that run at the same time, then combined /debate The crew argues over several rounds until they agree /spawn [...] A specialist robot answers it /delegate /del The chief plans steps, assigns them to crewmates, and they work through them in order /concurrent /conc Your MCP servers are split across robots that work at the same time (see MCP Servers) /orchestrate /orch A three-level build from a requirements document

docs.title: /verify: get a second opinion
docs.text:
Two robots on your current model answer the question independently. A third robot, the reconciler, compares the answers, notes where they agree and disagree, and writes a final answer that flags anything uncertain.

> /verify
> What's the time complexity of Python's list.sort() on nearly-sorted data?
Running verification (2 independent + reconciliation)...

Use it for factual or technical questions where a confident but wrong answer would be costly. It makes three requests instead of one.

docs.title: /decompose: split a big question
docs.text:
The chief breaks your message into two to five independent sub-tasks. AIA runs them all at the same time and then combines the results into one answer.

> /decompose
> Compare PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite for a small SaaS app: licensing, replication, and operational cost.
Decomposing prompt into sub-tasks...
Decomposed into 3 sub-tasks:
  1. Compare licensing of PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite ...
  2. Compare replication options ...
  3. Compare operational cost ...
Synthesizing results...

AIA then prints how long each part took and how much time running them in parallel saved:

Benchmark:
  Decompose probe : 1.42s
  Sub-task 1      : 4.10s
  Sub-task 2      : 5.02s
  Sub-task 3      : 3.87s
  Synthesis       : 3.31s
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  Sub-tasks serial est. : 13.00s  (sum of sub-task times)
  Sub-tasks concurrent  : 5.05s  (2.6x parallel speedup)
  Total flow wall time  : 9.80s  (compare against --tokens Time for a normal run)

With --tokens, AIA also shows the combined token use of all the parts. If the question can't usefully be split, AIA says Prompt cannot be meaningfully decomposed. Running normally. and answers it as usual. Sub-tasks can use your tools and MCP servers.

docs.title: /debate: let the crew argue
docs.text:
Every crew member answers. Then, round after round, each one reads the others' previous answers and responds. The debate ends when every robot says it agrees (by including the word CONVERGED), when a round's answers are very similar to the last round's, or after five rounds. There are always at least two rounds.

aia --chat -m gpt-4o-mini,claude-haiku-4-5

> /debate
> Should a small team adopt microservices from day one?
Debate between Tobor, Zen...
  Round 1: Tobor...
  Round 1: Zen...
  ...
  Converged in round 3.

You get every round, labelled by robot:

### Round 1
**Tobor**: ...
**Zen**: ...
### Round 2
...

You need at least two robots: several -m models, or crewmates you added with /add_recruit. If a robot fails in a round, its entry shows [FAILED] and the others carry on.

docs.title: /spawn: call in a specialist
docs.text:
/spawn creates a specialist robot to answer your next message. It doesn't join the crew; see Crews.

/spawn                                   # let the chief decide what kind of specialist
/spawn <type>                            # e.g. /spawn security_expert
/spawn <name> <provider/model> [skill:<id>...] <system prompt...>

> /spawn
Spawn mode enabled (auto-detect) for next prompt.
> What are the tax implications of an 83(b) election?
Determining specialist type...
Specialist 'tax_attorney' responding...
  • With no argument, the chief picks a specialist role and writes its instructions.
  • With a type, the specialist is told it's a <type> specialist.
  • The full form chooses the name, the model and the instructions. Use - or inherit as the model to keep the chief's model. The model can be on a different provider from the chief, for example a hosted expert in a local-model chat. skill:<id> adds a skill's text to the specialist's instructions, as it does for recruits.

AIA keeps up to five specialists per session and reuses one when you ask for the same role again. Specialists get the chief's tools and MCP servers, under the same tool-approval setting.

docs.title: /delegate: plan and hand off
docs.text:
The chief splits your request into steps and assigns each step to a crew member, choosing by their models. The members then work through the steps in order, and each step can see the results of the earlier ones.

> /add_recruit writer
> /add_recruit editor anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 You are a strict copy editor.
> /delegate
> Write a 300-word announcement for our 2.0 release, then tighten it.
Tobor analyzing and delegating...
Plan with 2 tasks:
  1. Draft the announcement -> writer
  2. Edit for clarity and length -> editor
  writer: Draft the announcement...
  editor: Edit for clarity and length...

The result lists every step with its assignee:

### Step 1: Draft the announcement (writer)
...
### Step 2: Edit for clarity and length (editor)
...

The plan is recorded as a short-lived plan in TrakFlow. If the chief names a member that doesn't exist, the step goes to the chief.

docs.title: /orchestrate: a three-level build
docs.text:
/orchestrate is for large jobs such as building a small application from a requirements document. Your next message is treated as the requirements.

  1. Tobor, the chief, splits the requirements into three to five architectural layers, such as infrastructure, data models, routes and views.
  2. A lead robot for each layer breaks its layer into up to four concrete tasks and names a specialist for each. All the leads work at the same time.
  3. A specialist for each task writes the actual file: code, a migration, a spec. All the specialists work at the same time.
  4. Each lead summarizes its layer, and Tobor writes a final integration report.
> /orchestrate
Orchestration mode enabled. Your next prompt is the application requirements.
> TaskFlow: a multi-user project and task manager. Ruby, Sinatra, Sequel (SQLite), ERB views. Users can sign up, create projects, ...

Type or paste the whole requirements document as that one message.

Everything is written to a new directory in the current folder, orchestrated_build_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS/, including INTEGRATION_REPORT.md:

Integration report: /Users/me/work/orchestrated_build_20261101_142233/INTEGRATION_REPORT.md
Build complete: /Users/me/work/orchestrated_build_20261101_142233

Warning

This mode sends many requests, most of them at the same time. Use a capable model, keep an eye on --cost, and review the generated files before you use them.

A system prompt that tells the chief when to use /spawn, /decompose and /delegate works well together with this mode. Set one with --system-prompt or prompts.system_prompt in your config file.

docs.title: Task tracking with TrakFlow
docs.text: AIA uses TrakFlow, a small local task tracker, to record plans and tasks. A TrakFlow project is marked by a .trak_flow directory. AIA starts TrakFlow only when a feature needs it: a task directive below, /spawn or /delegate work, --track-pipeline, or a model using the task-board tools. Then it looks for a .trak_flow directory in the current directory and its parents, and creates one in the current directory if it finds none. A session that uses none of these leaves nothing behind. The tasks themselves go in TrakFlow's database, which by default is ~/.config/trak_flow/tf.db, shared by every project.

docs.title: Directives
docs.text:
Directive Effect /tasks (alias /tf) List ready tasks (tasks with no open blockers) /tasks summary Count tasks by status /task <title> Create a task /plan <description> Create a task from a description 
> /task Write release notes for 2.0
Task created: [tf-a1b2] Write release notes for 2.0
> /tasks
Ready tasks (1):
  - [tf-a1b2] Write release notes for 2.0 (open)

/spawn and /delegate also record their work there. TrakFlow's own tf command lets you view and manage the same tasks outside AIA.

docs.title: Tracking a pipeline
docs.text:
--track-pipeline records a pipeline run as a TrakFlow plan, with one step per prompt. Each step is marked in progress, completed or blocked (with the error) as AIA works through it. A prompt that appears twice in the pipeline gets two steps, and each run updates its own. Without --track-pipeline, a pipeline run doesn't touch TrakFlow:

aia --track-pipeline research --pipeline outline,draft

docs.title: Crews
docs.text: Every AIA chat is backed by a crew: a small team of robots that share the conversation. With a single model, the crew has one member. You can recruit more members in the middle of a chat, address each one by name, and have them build on each other's answers.

docs.title: The chief and its crewmates
docs.text:
• The chief is the robot you started with. With one model it's named Tobor. It answers your normal messages, and it's the robot that /spawn builds specialists from.
  • Crewmates (recruits) are robots you add during the chat. Each has a name, a model and its own instructions, and answers to @name.

If you start with several models (aia --chat -m gpt-4o-mini,claude-haiku-4-5), each model is a crew member. The first one is still Tobor and is the chief, and the others are named after their model family (Zen, Spark, ...). Your messages then go to all of them; see Multiple Models.

Use /robots to see the crew, each member's model, and its @ handle:

> /robots

docs.title: Addressing crewmates with @mentions
docs.text:
Start a message with @name to send it to that crewmate instead of the chief. Names aren't case-sensitive.

> @critic Does this API design have any obvious flaws?

Only the named robot replies. AIA removes the leading @critic before passing the message on. An @word that names nobody is ordinary text and goes to the chief with the rest of the message, so you can write an email address or @deprecated freely. If the message starts with an @name that matches no one, AIA assumes a typo, reports it and sends nothing:

Unknown robot: @critc  (available: Tobor, researcher, critic)

docs.title: Several crewmates at once
docs.text:
Where you put the mentions changes how the crewmates run:

  • Mentions only at the start: they run at the same time. Each replies independently.

    > @researcher @critic what are the trade-offs of optimistic locking?

  • A mention inside the message: they run one after another. The mentioned crewmates take turns, and each reply is passed to the others before their turn, so later crewmates build on earlier answers.

    > draft a plan @researcher then have @critic poke holes in it

    Here @researcher answers first, and @critic sees that draft before replying.

docs.title: Broadcasting to the whole crew
docs.text:
@crew sends the message to every member at once:

> @crew in one sentence, what is your specialty?

Because crew is reserved for broadcasting, no member can be named crew.

Local models and broadcasts

Broadcasts and leading mentions send several requests at the same time. If every crewmate uses the same local model server, the requests queue up there and can time out. Raise the server's parallelism (for Ollama, OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL), give each crewmate a smaller task, or use a mention inside the message so they run one at a time.

docs.title: Recruiting crewmates
docs.text:
/add_recruit (alias /add) adds a crewmate that stays for the rest of the session:

/add_recruit <name> [provider/model] [skill:<id>...] [system prompt...]

# Same model as the chief, default instructions
> /add_recruit researcher

# A specific model and instructions
> /add_recruit critic anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 You are a ruthless design critic. Find flaws.

# A local model
> /add_recruit quick ollama/llama3.2 You are concise and fast.
  • name is required and must be unique (and not crew).
  • provider/model is optional. Leave it out to use the chief's model. Use - or inherit as a placeholder when you want the chief's model and want to write instructions.
  • Everything after the model is the crewmate's system prompt. Without one, the crewmate is simply told You are <name>.

AIA confirms the recruit:

Recruited 'critic' into the crew (anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5).

Recruits get the chief's tools and share its MCP server connections, so they can do the same work as the chief. Tool approvals follow your --tool-approval setting.

Switching models with /model rebuilds the crew from the new model list, so recruits don't survive the switch. Recruit them again afterwards.

docs.title: Giving a crewmate a role with skills
docs.text:
A crew of identical robots gives you identical answers. Give each crewmate a skill, a reusable set of instructions from your skills directory (list them with /skills; see Roles and Skills):

# A skill as the role
> /add_recruit reviewer skill:security-review

# A skill, a model, and an extra instruction
> /add_recruit reviewer ollama/llama3.2 skill:security-review focus on the auth module

# Several skills (repeat the token or separate with commas)
> /add_recruit reviewer - skill:security-review,ruby-style

skill:<id> can appear anywhere after the name. The crewmate's instructions are the skills' text followed by any system prompt you add. If a skill can't be found, the recruit fails with a message naming the missing skill, so you never get a crewmate without the role you meant to give it.

This turns @crew from four copies of the same answer into real division of labour, for example a security reviewer, a performance reviewer, a test reviewer and a style reviewer.

docs.title: Re-skilling a crewmate
docs.text:
/reskill gives a crewmate a fresh conversation and new instructions. It keeps its name and model:

> /reskill reviewer skill:test-writing
> /reskill reviewer you now summarize the other members' findings

Use it to bring a crewmate that wandered off task back on track, or to move the crew from one phase to the next (review, then fix, then summarize). The chief can't be re-skilled.

docs.title: Dropping a crewmate
docs.text:
> /drop_recruit researcher        # alias: /drop
Dropped 'researcher' from the crew.

The chief can't be dropped.

docs.title: Letting the chief recruit
docs.text:
The chief has two built-in tools for managing the crew: one to recruit a robot (name, optional model, optional skills, optional instructions) and one to reskill a member. So you can simply ask:

> Put together a review team: one robot for security, one for performance,
  each using the matching skill, then have them review lib/payment.rb.

The chief may recruit the members itself. Run /robots to see what it created. These tools show up in /tools as AIA::RecruitRobotTool and AIA::ReskillRobotTool. If you limit tools with --allowed-tools, include recruit and reskill in the list or the chief loses them.

docs.title: Recruits versus spawned specialists
docs.text:
/spawn (see Advanced Modes) also creates a robot, but for a different purpose:

/add_recruit /spawn Handles Every message you send it with @name Only your next message Joins the crew Yes: listed in /robots, reachable with @name No Tools and MCP servers The chief's The chief's Good for A standing teammate A one-off expert answer

Both accept the same name provider/model instructions form. If you keep spawning the same specialist, recruit it instead.

docs.title: Images and Speech
docs.text: AIA can turn a prompt into an image instead of text, and it can read chat replies out loud.

docs.title: Generating images with --paint
docs.text:
Add --paint and AIA sends each prompt to an image model instead of a chat model:

aia --paint logo_idea

echo "A lighthouse on a rocky coast at dusk, oil painting" > ~/.prompts/lighthouse.md
aia --paint lighthouse

By default the image is saved next to your output file with a .png extension. The default output file is temp.md, so the image lands in temp.png:

Image saved to: temp.png

Choose the file with -o:

aia --paint -o images/lighthouse.md lighthouse    # writes images/lighthouse.png

With --no-output nothing is saved. AIA prints the image URL the provider returned instead, or (image returned no URL) if the provider sent the image data directly. Keep an output file when you use a model that returns image data rather than a URL.

Everything you know about prompts still applies: parameters, directives, ERB and shell, and pipelines (each prompt in a pipeline makes its own image). --paint applies to prompts you run from the command line, not to chat sessions.

docs.title: Image options
docs.text:
Option Config key Default Meaning --im, --image-model MODEL image.model gpt-image-1 The image model --is, --image-size SIZE image.size 1024x1024 Image dimensions --iq, --image-quality QUALITY image.quality standard Quality setting --style, --image-style STYLE image.style vivid Style setting 
aia --paint --im gpt-image-1 --is 1536x1024 --iq hd --style natural lighthouse

Which sizes, qualities and styles are accepted depends on the model and provider. Check the provider's documentation. To find image-capable models:

aia --available-models text_to_image

Available LLMs for text_to_image:

- gpt-image-1 (azure) text,image to image
...

text_to_image matches models that take text and return an image. Add a provider name to narrow it: --available-models text_to_image,openai.

docs.title: Hearing replies with --speak
docs.text:
--speak reads replies aloud: every reply in a chat, including replies from crewmates you address with @name, the reply to a one-shot prompt, and each step of a pipeline:

aia --chat --speak
aia --chat --speak --voice Samantha
aia --speak daily_briefing

Images from --paint aren't spoken.

docs.title: The default: macOS say
docs.text: By default AIA speaks with the macOS say command. --voice picks one of its voices; run say -v '?' to list them. Config keys: flags.speak, audio.voice.

docs.title: Using your own text-to-speech command
docs.text:
To use a cloud voice or another text-to-speech engine, point --speak-command at your own script:

aia --chat --speak --speak-command ~/bin/tts.sh

AIA runs the command with two arguments: the text to speak, and the path of an .mp3 file to write. When the command has written that file, AIA plays it with audio.player. If you haven't set one, AIA uses the first of afplay (built into macOS), mpv, ffplay and mpg123 that it finds on your PATH, and warns if it finds none. For example:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ~/bin/tts.sh TEXT OUTPUT_FILE
text="$1"; out="$2"
curl -s https://api.openai.com/v1/audio/speech \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "$(jq -n --arg t "$text" --arg m "${SPEECH_MODEL:-tts-1}" \
        '{model:$m, voice:"alloy", input:$t}')" \
  -o "$out"

--speech-model (--sm) is handed to your command as the SPEECH_MODEL environment variable. AIA doesn't use it any other way. The config key for the command is audio.speak_command (default say).

To choose the player yourself, set audio.player in your config file or AIA_AUDIO__PLAYER in the environment. The value is a command line; AIA adds the file path at the end:

audio:
  speak_command: ~/bin/tts.sh
  player: mpv --no-video --really-quiet

docs.title: Speaking a single line: /say
docs.text:
In a chat, /say speaks the text you give it using the macOS say command and your --voice. Nothing is sent to the model:

> /say The build is finished.

docs.title: Transcription model
docs.text: --transcription-model (--tm, config audio.transcription_model) sets the default model RubyLLM uses for speech-to-text. AIA itself doesn't take voice input. The setting is there for tools that transcribe audio.

docs.title: Local Models and Providers
docs.text: AIA works with any provider that RubyLLM supports, including models running on your own machine with Ollama or LM Studio. Local models keep your prompts on your computer, work offline and cost nothing per request.

docs.title: Providers and the provider/ prefix
docs.text:
A provider is a service that serves models: OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, Ollama and so on. To pick a provider explicitly, put its name in front of the model:

aia -m ollama/llama3.2 my_prompt
aia -m openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 my_prompt

AIA treats the text before the first / as a provider only if RubyLLM knows a provider by that name. Model IDs that already contain a slash, such as meta-llama/llama-4-maverick, are left alone.

To see which providers are available, and which ones already have an API key set, run:

$ aia --list-providers
Registered RubyLLM providers:
------------------------------------------------------------
- anthropic
- gemini (has API key)
- lms (local)
- ollama (local)
- openai (has API key)
- openrouter (has API key)
...

A provider counts as "has API key" when <PROVIDER>_API_KEY is set, for example OPENAI_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

docs.title: A default provider
docs.text:
If you use one provider all the time, set it with --provider and leave off the prefix:

aia --provider ollama -m llama3.2 my_prompt

A model that has its own prefix keeps it. --provider also tells --list-models which provider to ask:

$ aia --provider ollama --list-models

ollama models:
------------------------------------------------------------
- ollama/llama3.2:latest
- ollama/qwen3:8b

2 ollama model(s) available

--list-models asks the provider's server what it has right now. --available-models searches RubyLLM's built-in model catalogue instead, which mostly covers hosted models (see Choosing Models).

docs.title: Provider gems
docs.text: Some providers ship as separate gems named ruby_llm-providers-<name>. Install the gem and use its prefix: AIA loads it the first time it sees that prefix. You can also load one explicitly with --require (--rq). --list-providers lists every installed provider gem.

docs.title: Custom endpoints
docs.text:
For every provider, an environment variable named <PROVIDER>_API_BASE overrides the provider's endpoint, as long as the provider supports a custom endpoint:

export OLLAMA_API_BASE=http://gpu-box.local:11434/v1
export LMS_API_BASE=http://localhost:1234/v1

docs.title: Ollama
docs.text:
1. Install Ollama and download a model:

    brew install ollama        # macOS; see ollama.com for other systems
ollama serve               # if it isn't already running
ollama pull llama3.2

  2. Use the ollama/ prefix. AIA expects Ollama at http://localhost:11434/v1; if it runs elsewhere, set OLLAMA_API_BASE (see Custom endpoints):

    aia -m ollama/llama3.2 my_prompt
aia --chat -m ollama/llama3.2
aia --provider ollama --list-models

docs.title: LM Studio
docs.text:
1. Install LM Studio, download a model, and start its local server (it listens on http://localhost:1234/v1 by default).

  2. Install the LM Studio provider gem:

    gem install ruby_llm-providers-lms

  3. Use the lms/ prefix with the model ID that LM Studio shows:

    aia -m lms/qwen/qwen3-coder-30b my_prompt
aia --provider lms --list-models

The LM Studio provider talks to http://localhost:1234/v1 unless you set LMS_API_BASE. It needs no API key.

docs.title: Mixing local and cloud models
docs.text:
Local and hosted models can be combined in the same session:

# Compare a local model with a hosted one
aia -m ollama/llama3.2,gpt-4o-mini my_prompt

# A local chief, plus a hosted crewmate recruited during the chat
aia --chat -m ollama/llama3.2
> /add_recruit expert anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 You answer the hard questions.

A crewmate or /spawn specialist with an explicit provider/model uses that provider, even when the chief is local. See Crews.

docs.title: Listing models from a chat
docs.text:
/available_models (also /models, /am, /llms) lists models from a chat. If your current models carry a provider prefix, it asks that provider's server for its live model list. Otherwise it searches RubyLLM's catalogue. Add words to filter the list:

> /models qwen

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Pick a model that fits your hardware. Smaller models answer faster, and larger ones follow instructions and call tools more reliably. Agent-style features (tools, /decompose, /orchestrate) need a model that's good at following instructions.
  • Concurrent requests queue up. Multi-model runs, @crew broadcasts, /debate and /decompose send several requests at the same time. A single local server handles only a few at once, and the rest wait. For Ollama, raise OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL, or run fewer things at once.
  • There's no price for local models. --cost shows costs only for models that RubyLLM has prices for. Token counts (--tokens) still work.
  • Timeouts. Each model request may take up to 120 seconds. Long generations on a slow machine can go over that; a shorter prompt or a smaller model helps.

docs.title: MCP Servers
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way for programs to offer tools to an AI. Connect AIA to an MCP server, such as a filesystem server, a GitHub server or a database server, and the model can call that server's tools just like local tools.

AIA supports MCP servers that run as a local process (stdio) and servers you reach over HTTP (Streamable HTTP). The older SSE and WebSocket transports aren't supported.

docs.title: Configuring a server in your config file
docs.text:
List servers under mcp_servers in ~/.config/aia/aia.yml (or in any file you pass with -c):

mcp_servers:
  - name: filesystem
    command: npx
    args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/Users/me/projects"]
    timeout: 10000

Every server you configure is connected at startup, so its tools are available in every session.

Key Meaning name The name you use with --mcp-use, --mcp-skip and /mcp command, args The program to start, for stdio servers env Extra environment variables for the server process, such as API tokens cwd (or directory) Working directory for the server process url The endpoint of an HTTP server. If you give a url, the server uses Streamable HTTP headers, bearer_token, oauth Authentication for HTTP servers timeout How long to wait for the server to connect (see below) prefix A prefix added to every tool name from this server only, except Lists of tool names to keep or drop from this server requires_approval Make tool calls wait for your approval (see below) group Concurrency grouping (see Running servers concurrently)

An HTTP server with a token:

mcp_servers:
  - name: tracker
    url: https://mcp.example.com/mcp
    headers:
      Authorization: "Bearer <your-token>"

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
timeout sets how long AIA waits for one server to connect and report its tools. Values of 1000 or more are milliseconds and smaller values are seconds, so 10000 and 10 both mean ten seconds. Without a timeout, a server gets 30 seconds.

All servers connect at the same time. The whole connection phase is also capped by concurrency.mcp_timeout (default 120 seconds), but never at less than your slowest server's own timeout. Servers started with npx or uvx can be slow the first time they download, so give them a generous timeout.

docs.title: Naming a server class
docs.text:
An entry in mcp_servers: can also be the name of a RubyLLM::MCP subclass. The class describes its own command or URL, environment and timeout, so the entry needs nothing else. Load the file that defines the class with require_libs: (or --require); AIA loads those libraries before it connects any server.

require_libs:
  - shared_tools
  - shared_tools/mcp

mcp_servers:
  - SharedTools::MCP::Memory
  - SharedTools::MCP::GitHub
  - name: filesystem              # Hash entries still work alongside them
    command: npx
    args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "."]

The server is known by the class's default name (SharedTools::MCP::GitHub is github), which is the name to use with --mcp-use and --mcp-skip. If the class has an available? method that returns false, as the shared_tools classes do when their API key is missing, AIA skips the server and says why. Example 30 in the repository uses every shared_tools server this way.

docs.title: Loading servers from a JSON file
docs.text:
--mcp FILE reads servers from a JSON file in the format used by Claude Desktop and VS Code. You can repeat it, and the servers are added to the ones in your config file:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "./docs"],
      "timeout": 10000
    }
  }
}

aia --mcp ~/mcp/filesystem.json --chat
aia --mcp github.json --mcp postgres.json my_prompt

A file without an mcpServers key is read as one server, named after the file: {"command": "my-server", "args": ["--stdio"]}. Here command may also be an array whose first element is the program. Both forms accept the same keys.

A server in a JSON file can use every key a server in the YAML config can: command, args, env, url, headers, type, timeout, group, prefix, only, except and requires_approval. A url with no type is a Streamable HTTP server.

docs.title: Choosing servers for a session
docs.text:
Option Effect --mcp-use NAMES (--mu) Connect only the named servers (comma-separated, repeatable) --mcp-skip NAMES (--ms) Connect every server except these --no-mcp Connect no MCP servers at all --mcp-list List the configured servers and exit 
aia --mcp-use filesystem,github --chat
aia --mcp-skip postgres my_prompt
aia --no-mcp quick_question

If a name given to --mcp-use doesn't match any configured server, AIA warns you and lists the names it knows:

WARNING: --mcp-use specified server(s) not found in config: githb
         Available servers: filesystem, github

--mcp-list shows what's configured, after --mcp-use and --mcp-skip are applied:

$ aia --mcp-list
Configured MCP servers:

  filesystem
    command: npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /Users/me/projects

To see each server's tools, add --list-tools:

aia --list-tools --mcp-list

The config file equivalents are mcp_use, mcp_skip and flags.no_mcp.

docs.title: What happens at startup
docs.text:
AIA starts every selected server at once and shows a spinner line for each:

[✔] Connecting MCP servers
  [✔] filesystem (14 tools)
  [✖] github (timed out)

A server that fails to connect is left out for the rest of the session, so AIA doesn't keep retrying it. Everything else carries on normally.

Inside a chat, /mcp shows the status of every server and the tools it offers:

> /mcp

MCP Server Status
=================
Defined: 2  Connected: 1  Failed: 1

Connected Servers:
  filesystem (14 tools)
    - read_file
    - list_directory
    ...

Failed Servers:
  github: timed out after 10.0s

Every robot in the session shares the same server connections, including crew members you recruit. Each server process starts only once.

docs.title: Requiring approval
docs.text:
To make a server's tool calls wait for your OK, set requires_approval in the YAML config:

mcp_servers:
  - name: filesystem
    command: npx
    args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "."]
    requires_approval: true                     # every tool
  - name: github
    command: github-mcp-server
    args: ["stdio"]
    requires_approval: [create_issue, merge_pull_request]   # only these tools

What happens next depends on --tool-approval (ask, approve or deny). Tools: approval explains the modes. In the same way, AIA asks you on the terminal when a server needs input from you, such as a value or a URL to visit.

docs.title: Two servers with the same tool name
docs.text:
Two tools can't share a name. When a server offers a tool with the same name as one from a server that's already connected, the second server is marked failed:

github: tool 'search' is also offered by 'gitlab'; give one server a prefix:

Fix this by giving one of the servers a prefix:

  - name: gitlab
    command: gitlab-mcp
    prefix: gitlab

docs.title: Running servers concurrently
docs.text:
When a question needs tools from several unrelated servers, AIA can split the work. One robot works with each group of servers, all at the same time, and a final robot merges their results.

  • In a chat, type /concurrent (or /conc) before your next message. That message is handled this way.
  • For prompts run from the command line, add --concurrent-auto, or set concurrency.auto: true in your config.

This happens only when there's more than one server. Servers that share the same group value stay together in one robot, and every server without a group gets its own. With --concurrent-auto, AIA splits the work only when there are at least concurrency.threshold groups (default 2). Otherwise the prompt runs normally.

mcp_servers:
  - name: github
    command: github-mcp-server
    args: ["stdio"]
  - name: postgres
    command: postgres-mcp
    group: data
  - name: redis
    command: redis-mcp
    group: data          # runs together with postgres
concurrency:
  auto: true
  threshold: 2
  mcp_timeout: 120

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• A server shows (timed out). Raise its timeout. The first npx -y ... run downloads the package and can take a while. Running the command yourself in a terminal shows whether it starts at all.
  • A server shows an error message. Check command, args and env. The message is the error the server reported. Run with --log-level debug (or -d) for connection details. MCP activity goes to the MCP log; see Configuration keys for logger.mcp.
  • --mcp-use gives no tools. Check the warning about names that weren't found. Server names are case-sensitive.
  • The model ignores a server's tools in chat. AIA's automatic tool filter may not have matched your message to them. Mention what you want done more explicitly, or turn the filter off with --no-auto-tool-filter.
  • Too many tools. Use only:/except: on the server, or --allowed-tools/--rejected-tools.

docs.title: Multiple Models and Consensus
docs.text: AIA can send one prompt to several models at once. You can read their answers side by side, or have one model merge them into a single consensus answer. In a chat you can also switch models without losing the conversation.

docs.title: Asking several models at once
docs.text:
Give --model (-m) a comma-separated list:

aia -m gpt-4o-mini,claude-haiku-4-5 explain_recursion

All the models run in parallel. Each answer is labelled with the robot's name, its model and how long it took:

**Tobor [gpt-4o-mini]** (2.1s):
Recursion is when a function calls itself...

**Zen [claude-haiku-4-5]** (1.8s):
A recursive function solves a problem by...

The first robot is always named Tobor. The others are named after their model family (Spark for gpt-4o-mini, Zen for Claude Haiku, Lyric for Claude Sonnet 4, Prism for Gemini Flash, and so on). If two robots would get the same name, the second gets a number (Zen2). These names are the handles you use with @mentions in chat; see Crews.

In the config file, list the models under models:

models:
  - name: gpt-4o-mini
  - name: claude-haiku-4-5

Models can include a provider prefix, such as ollama/llama3.2 or openai/gpt-4o. See Local Models and Choosing Models.

docs.title: Consensus: one merged answer
docs.text:
Add --consensus and the individual answers go to a synthesizer robot named Weaver. Weaver combines the best points into one answer:

aia --consensus -m gpt-4o-mini,claude-haiku-4-5,gemini-2.5-flash explain_recursion

Weaver uses the first model in your list, so put the model you trust most for writing first. The output shows each model's answer followed by Weaver's merged answer under the consensus label.

--no-consensus turns it off again (useful when your config file sets flags.consensus: true).

docs.title: Giving each model a role
docs.text:
A role is a prompt file in your roles directory (~/.prompts/roles/ by default) that shapes how a model behaves. You can give each model its own role with MODEL=ROLE:

aia -m gpt-4o=architect,claude-sonnet-4-5=security_reviewer review_design design.md

AIA stops with an error if a role file doesn't exist. The role is added to that model's system prompt, so the same question gets an architect's answer and a security reviewer's answer.

The same model can appear more than once with different roles:

aia -m gpt-4o-mini=optimist,gpt-4o-mini=pessimist forecast

In YAML:

models:
  - name: gpt-4o
    role: architect
  - name: claude-sonnet-4-5
    role: security_reviewer

Roles and Skills explains how roles are written.

docs.title: Multiple models in chat
docs.text:
aia --chat -m gpt-4o-mini,claude-haiku-4-5

Each message you type goes to every model, and their answers show up together, or merged if you used --consensus. To talk to just one of them, address it by name:

> @zen what do you think of Tobor's answer?

/robots lists the models in the session and their names. Crews covers @mentions and adding more members.

For a more structured exchange, use /debate (the models answer each other over several rounds) or /verify (two independent answers plus a reconciliation). Both are described in Advanced Modes.

docs.title: Switching models during a chat
docs.text:
/model with no argument shows the current model or models. Give it model names to switch:

> /model
> /model claude-sonnet-4-5
Switching to claude-sonnet-4-5 (conversation: summarize)...
> /model gpt-4o-mini,claude-haiku-4-5

How the conversation is carried over is set by model_switch_history in your config file (or AIA_MODEL_SWITCH_HISTORY):

Value What the new model gets summarize (default) The old model writes a summary of the conversation, and the new model starts from that summary. This costs one request for the summary, plus one request per new model to hand it over. replay Every message you sent is re-sent to the new model, one at a time. The most faithful option, but one request per message you typed, per new model. clean Nothing. The new model starts fresh. 
model_switch_history: replay

The switch rebuilds the crew from the new model list, so crewmates you added with /add_recruit are dropped. See Crews.

Tools and MCP servers are turned off while AIA replays or summarizes, so the transfer can't cause side effects.

Note

Use /model to switch. It takes model names or aliases such as sonnet or cheap (see /model). Typing a request such as "switch to claude" goes to the model as an ordinary message.

docs.title: Costs and timing
docs.text: Several models means several bills. Add --tokens to see token counts and response time after each turn, or --cost to see the price as well. See Output and History.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tools let the model do things while it answers: read the clock, look up DNS records, count words, query a database. You load them when you start AIA, and the model decides when to call them.

AIA can use any tool written for RubyLLM, meaning a Ruby class that subclasses RubyLLM::Tool. You can load tools from a gem, from your own .rb files, or from MCP servers (see MCP Servers).

docs.title: Loading tools from a gem
docs.text:
Use --require (short form --rq) to load a gem at startup. AIA finds every tool the gem defines and gives them to the model.

The shared_tools gem has a ready-made collection:

gem install shared_tools

aia --rq shared_tools --chat

Some of the tools it provides:

Tool name What it does current_date_time_tool Current date, time and time zone system_info_tool OS, CPU, memory and disk details dns_tool DNS lookups cron_tool Parse and explain cron expressions calculator Arithmetic weather_tool Weather lookups disk_tool File and directory operations clipboard_tool Read or write the system clipboard doc_tool, database_tool, browser_tool, computer_tool, ... More specialised tools

To load several gems, separate them with commas (--rq shared_tools,my_tools) or repeat the option. To load gems every time, put them in your config file:

# ~/.config/aia/aia.yml
require_libs:
  - shared_tools

Some tools act on your machine

Tools such as disk_tool, computer_tool and eval_tool can change files or run code. Load only the tools you trust, and use --allowed-tools to keep the list short. See Security.

docs.title: Loading your own tool files
docs.text:
Use --tools to load .rb files directly. You can pass a single file, a directory (AIA loads every *.rb file in it), or a comma-separated list of either:

aia --tools ~/my_tools/word_count_tool.rb my_prompt
aia --tools ~/my_tools --chat
aia --tools ~/my_tools,./project_tools --chat

AIA exits with an error if a path doesn't exist, or if you name a file that doesn't end in .rb.

To load the same files every time, list them in your config file:

tools:
  paths:
    - ~/my_tools/word_count_tool.rb

docs.title: Writing a simple tool
docs.text:
A tool is a small Ruby class. Give it a name, a description the model can read, its parameters, and an execute method that returns a result:

# ~/my_tools/word_count_tool.rb
require 'ruby_llm/tool'

class WordCountTool < RubyLLM::Tool
  def self.name = 'word_count'

  description <<~DESC
    Count words, characters, lines, and sentences in a given text.
    Useful for text analysis and content length checks.
  DESC

  parameter :text, type: :string, description: 'The text to analyze', required: true

  def execute(text:)
    words     = text.split(/\s+/).reject(&:empty?)
    sentences = text.split(/[.!?]+/).reject { |s| s.strip.empty? }

    { words: words.size, characters: text.length,
      lines: text.lines.size, sentences: sentences.size }
  end
end

Then ask for it in a prompt:

aia --tools ~/my_tools/word_count_tool.rb --chat

> Use the word_count tool on this: "Ruby is a dynamic, open source programming language."

Some tips:

  • Write the description for the model. The model chooses tools by their descriptions, and AIA's automatic tool filter (below) matches your prompt against them too. Say plainly what the tool does and when to use it.
  • Return data, not prose. A Hash or String is fine; the model turns it into an answer.
  • Raise or return an error message when something goes wrong. The model sees the error and can explain it or try again.
  • A tool can define an available? method. If it returns false, AIA skips the tool at startup and prints Info: Tool '<name>' is not available, skipping.

See the RubyLLM tools guide for parameter types and other details.

docs.title: Seeing which tools are loaded
docs.text:
From the command line, --list-tools prints your local tools and exits:

aia --tools ~/my_tools --list-tools

Add --mcp-list to include the tools offered by your MCP servers, grouped by server:

aia --list-tools --mcp-list

On a terminal the list is plain text. When you pipe it or redirect it to a file, it's Markdown:

aia --list-tools --mcp-list > tools.md

Inside a chat, /tools lists every loaded tool, local and MCP. Give it a word to filter by name or description:

> /tools
> /tools dns

Your AIA crew-management tools (AIA::RecruitRobotTool and AIA::ReskillRobotTool) always show up in these lists. They let the model add crewmates on its own; see Crews.

--list-tools loads tools the way a session does, including gems such as shared_tools that load their tools lazily, and applies --allowed-tools and --rejected-tools (below). /tools shows everything that's loaded, not only what the model is allowed to use.

docs.title: Limiting which tools the model sees
docs.text:
Large tool collections can confuse a model, and some models stop calling tools at all when they get dozens of them. Narrow the set down:

# Only these tools
aia --rq shared_tools \
    --allowed-tools current_date_time_tool,system_info_tool,dns_tool \
    my_prompt

# Everything except these
aia --rq shared_tools --rejected-tools computer_tool,eval_tool --chat

The short forms are --at and --rt. A few details:

  • Matching is a case-insensitive substring match on the tool name, so --allowed-tools date keeps current_date_time_tool.
  • Both options take comma-separated lists and can be repeated.
  • If you use both, --allowed-tools is applied first and --rejected-tools then removes from what's left.
  • The crew-management tools are filtered like any other tool. --allowed-tools drops them unless one of your terms matches their names (for example recruit or reskill), and then the chief can't recruit crewmates on its own.

The config file equivalents are tools.allowed and tools.rejected.

docs.title: Automatic tool filtering in chat
docs.text:
In a chat session AIA picks the tools that fit each turn. It compares your message with every tool's name, description and parameter names (local and MCP tools alike) and sends the model only the tools that score high enough, up to 30 per turn. This is on by default.

  • When no tool matches a turn, the model gets no tools for that turn. This keeps a large tool set from going over a provider's limit on tools per request. If the model ignores a tool you expected it to use, name the tool or describe what it does in your message.
  • To see which tools were chosen for each turn, run with --verbose or --debug:
Filtered tools (2): current_date_time_tool, dns_tool
  • Turn it off to always send every allowed tool:
aia --no-auto-tool-filter --chat

The config file key is flags.auto_tool_filter: false.

docs.title: Tools that need your approval
docs.text:
Some tool calls must be approved before they run. That happens when an MCP server is configured with requires_approval (see MCP Servers), or when a tool declares that it needs approval (with RubyLLM's requires_approval). MCP servers can also ask you for input mid-task.

--tool-approval decides what happens:

Mode Behaviour ask (default) AIA stops and asks on the terminal. With no terminal (for example in a script or pipe), the call is refused. approve Every call that needs approval runs without asking. MCP input requests are still asked on the terminal. deny Every call that needs approval is refused, and every MCP input request is declined.

In ask mode a prompt looks like this:

Tool 'delete_file' requires approval.
  arguments: path="notes/old.md"
  Allow it? [y/N]

Only y or yes approves the call. Questions go to stderr, so they don't mix with the model's answer.

When AIA refuses a call because nobody can answer, it says so:

[AIA] Refused: tool 'delete_file' requires approval and there is no terminal to ask. Set tools.approval (--tool-approval) to approve or deny.

Set the default in your config file with tools.approval: ask|approve|deny, or with the AIA_TOOLS__APPROVAL environment variable.

docs.title: Your First Prompt
docs.text: In this chapter you build one useful prompt, a code explainer, a step at a time. Along the way you meet the pieces every AIA prompt is made of: plain text, parameters, front matter, shell expansion, includes and chat.

docs.title: Step 1: A plain prompt
docs.text:
A prompt is just a Markdown file in your prompts directory (~/.prompts). Create ~/.prompts/explain_code.md:

~/.prompts/explain_code.md
Explain what the following code does, step by step.
Point out anything surprising or risky.

Run it, giving it a source file to explain:

aia --no-output explain_code app/models/user.rb

AIA reads the prompt file, appends the contents of app/models/user.rb, sends the result to the model, and prints the answer:

AI: 
   **Tobor** (3.1s):
   This file defines a `User` model with ...

The bold name is the robot that answered. AIA gives each model it runs a name; with a single model it's always Tobor.

Two things to notice:

  • The prompt ID is the file name without .md. A prompt in a subfolder includes the folder: ~/.prompts/dev/explain-code.md is dev/explain-code.
  • Extra arguments are context files. Everything after the prompt ID must be an existing file. AIA appends each one to the prompt.

About --no-output

Without it, AIA also writes the response to ./temp.md. That's handy when you want to keep an answer, and noise when you don't. You can turn it off permanently with output.file: ~ in your config file. See Output, History and Usage.

docs.title: Step 2: Add a parameter
docs.text:
Make the explanation fit your reader. Add YAML front matter with a parameters: section, and use the parameter in the text with ERB (<%= ... %>):

~/.prompts/explain_code.md
---
parameters:
  audience: a junior developer
---
Explain what the following code does, step by step, for <%= audience %>.
Point out anything surprising or risky.

Run it again. AIA now asks you for the value first:

$ aia --no-output explain_code app/models/user.rb
Value for audience (a junior developer):

Press Enter to accept the default in parentheses, or type something else (a product manager). A parameter whose default is empty (audience: with nothing after it) is required: AIA keeps it marked (required) and stops with an error if you don't give a value.

More in Parameters.

docs.title: Step 3: Choose the model when you run it
docs.text:
Pick the model with --model (-m) and tune how creative it is with --temperature (-t):

aia --no-output -m claude-sonnet-4-5 -t 0.3 explain_code app/models/user.rb

If you always want the same model, set it once in your config file instead. See Choosing Models.

docs.title: Step 4: Pull in live information
docs.text:
A prompt can run shell commands. $(command) is replaced with the command's output, and $VAR or ${VAR} with an environment variable:

~/.prompts/explain_code.md
---
parameters:
  audience: a junior developer
---
I'm working in a $(basename $(pwd)) project on $(uname -s).
The most recent commit touching these files was:

$(git log -1 --oneline)

Explain what the following code does, step by step, for <%= audience %>.
Point out anything surprising or risky.

Commands run when AIA loads the prompt, before anything is sent to the model. Because of that, only run prompts you trust. See ERB and Shell Expansion and Security.

docs.title: Step 5: Reuse text with include
docs.text:
If several prompts share the same guidance, keep it in one file and include it. Create ~/.prompts/includes/house_style.md:

~/.prompts/includes/house_style.md
Use short paragraphs. Show code in fenced blocks with a language tag.
Never invent APIs; say "I'm not sure" instead.

and add one line to the prompt:

<%= include 'includes/house_style.md' %>

include renders the other file (its own ERB and shell references are processed too). Use insert (alias read) instead to drop in a file's raw text untouched. See Directives.

docs.title: Step 6: Keep talking
docs.text:
When the first answer raises more questions, add --chat:

aia --chat explain_code app/models/user.rb

AIA runs the prompt as before, then leaves you at a follow-up prompt with the whole conversation still in context:

Follow up (cntl-D or 'exit' to end) #=>
Why is the callback on line 42 risky?

Type exit, press Ctrl+D, or press Enter on an empty line to finish. See Chat Sessions.

docs.title: Step 7: Keep comments out of the prompt
docs.text:
You can leave notes for yourself in a prompt file with HTML comments. They are stripped before the prompt is processed, so the model never sees them:

<!-- v2: added house style include, 2026-10-30 -->

docs.title: The finished prompt
docs.text:
~/.prompts/explain_code.md
---
parameters:
  audience: a junior developer
---
<!-- Explains a source file. Pass the file(s) as context. -->
I'm working in a $(basename $(pwd)) project on $(uname -s).
The most recent commit touching these files was:

$(git log -1 --oneline)

Explain what the following code does, step by step, for <%= audience %>.
Point out anything surprising or risky.

<%= include 'includes/house_style.md' %>

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This page gets AIA installed, connected to at least one model provider, and ready to run your first prompt. It takes about five minutes.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Requirement Notes Ruby 4.0.9 or later AIA 2.0 will not install on older Rubies. Check with ruby --version. An API key for at least one provider OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, and others. Or a local model server (Ollama, LM Studio) and no key at all. fzf (optional) Needed only for fuzzy prompt search (aia --fuzzy).

Managing Ruby versions

If your system Ruby is older than 4.0.9, install a newer one with a version manager such as rbenv, asdf, mise or chruby. AIA does not need system-wide Ruby.

docs.title: Install the gem
docs.text:
gem install aia

Check that it worked:

aia --version

2.0.0

docs.title: Connect a model provider
docs.text:
AIA reads provider API keys from environment variables. Set the one(s) for the providers you plan to use, in your ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc or equivalent:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
export GEMINI_API_KEY="..."

AIA also recognizes DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, MISTRAL_API_KEY, PERPLEXITY_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, XAI_API_KEY and GPUSTACK_API_KEY, the AWS variables for Bedrock (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_REGION, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN), and GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT / GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION for Vertex AI.

To see which providers AIA knows about and which of them have a key:

aia --list-providers

Registered RubyLLM providers:
------------------------------------------------------------
- anthropic (has API key)
- gemini
- ollama (local)
- openai (has API key)
...

The default model

Out of the box AIA uses OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini, so it needs OPENAI_API_KEY. If you use a different provider, either pass --model every time or set your own default in the config file (below). See Choosing Models.

Keep keys out of prompts and config files you share

Environment variables are the safest place for keys. See Security.

docs.title: Create your prompts directory
docs.text:
AIA looks for prompts in ~/.prompts. Create it, along with a folder for roles:

mkdir -p ~/.prompts/roles

If you'd rather keep prompts somewhere else (a git repository, a synced folder), point AIA at it:

export AIA_PROMPTS__DIR=~/Documents/prompts

or use --prompts-dir DIR on the command line, or set prompts.dir in the config file.

docs.title: Create a config file (optional)
docs.text:
You don't need a config file. AIA has sensible built-in defaults. When you want to change one permanently, create ~/.config/aia/aia.yml. A small starting point:

# ~/.config/aia/aia.yml
models:
  - name: claude-sonnet-4-5

prompts:
  dir: ~/.prompts

output:
  file: ~          # don't write responses to ./temp.md

Why output.file: ~?

By default AIA also writes every response to a file named temp.md in the current directory. Setting output.file to ~ (YAML for "nothing") turns that off. See Output, History and Usage.

You can capture the full set of settings AIA is using into a file to see what's available:

aia --dump my_settings.yml

Every key is described in the Configuration Keys reference.

docs.title: Shell completion (optional)
docs.text:
AIA can complete prompt IDs when you press Tab. It ships completion scripts for bash, zsh and fish:

bashzshfish 
aia --completion bash > ~/.aia_completion.bash
echo 'source ~/.aia_completion.bash' >> ~/.bashrc

aia --completion zsh > ~/.aia_completion.zsh
echo 'source ~/.aia_completion.zsh' >> ~/.zshrc

aia --completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/aia.fish

The completion scripts read your prompts directory from AIA_PROMPTS__DIR, so export it even if you use the default:

export AIA_PROMPTS__DIR=~/.prompts

docs.title: Install fzf (optional)
docs.text:
fzf lets you pick a prompt from a searchable list with a preview pane:

brew install fzf          # macOS
sudo apt install fzf      # Debian / Ubuntu

Then run aia --fuzzy (or aia -f). If fzf isn't installed, AIA tells you so and exits.

docs.title: Check that everything works
docs.text:
echo "Reply with the single word: ready" | aia --no-output

AI: 
   **Tobor** (0.8s):
   ready

If you see a response, you're done. If not:

Symptom Likely cause invalid option A typo in an option, or an option removed in 2.0. Run aia --help. An authentication / API key error The key for the model's provider isn't set in this shell. Run aia --list-providers. aia: command not found The gem's bin directory isn't on your PATH. Run gem environment and check EXECUTABLE DIRECTORY.

More fixes are in the FAQ and troubleshooting page.

docs.title: Upgrading from AIA 1.x
docs.text: AIA 2.0 is not a drop-in replacement for 1.x. Removed options, changed defaults and the new tool format are listed in Upgrading to 2.0. Older prompt files may need migrating.

docs.title: Quick Tour
docs.text:
A ten-minute walk through the things you'll do with AIA most often. Each stop links to the chapter that covers it in depth. You only need AIA installed and one API key (see Installation).

Follow along without clutter

The examples pass --no-output so AIA doesn't also write each answer to ./temp.md. If you've already set output.file: ~ in your config file, you can leave it off.

docs.title: 1. Ask a question
docs.text:
The fastest way to use AIA is to pipe a question into it:

echo "What does the Unix 'tee' command do? One sentence." | aia --no-output

AI: 
   **Tobor** (1.2s):
   `tee` reads standard input and writes it both to standard output and to one or more files.

When there's no prompt ID on the command line, whatever arrives on stdin is the prompt.

docs.title: 2. Save a prompt and run it by name
docs.text:
Prompts you use more than once belong in files. Create one in your prompts directory:

cat > ~/.prompts/explain.md <<'PROMPT'
Explain the following to a developer who is new to it.
Be brief, and give one concrete example.
PROMPT

The file name, without .md, is the prompt ID:

echo "Ruby's safe navigation operator" | aia --no-output explain

Now the prompt comes from the file and stdin is appended to it. See Running Prompts.

docs.title: 3. Give it files to work on
docs.text:
Any files listed after the prompt ID are added to the prompt as context:

aia --no-output explain lib/parser.rb

You can list as many files as you want. See Context Files and Piping.

docs.title: 4. Fill in parameters
docs.text:
A prompt can declare parameters in YAML front matter and use them with ERB:

~/.prompts/translate.md
---
parameters:
  language: Spanish
---
Translate the following text into <%= language %>. Keep the formatting.

echo "The meeting has moved to Thursday." | aia --no-output translate

Value for language (Spanish): French

AI: 
   **Tobor** (0.9s):
   La réunion a été déplacée à jeudi.

Press Enter to accept the default shown in parentheses. See Parameters.

docs.title: 5. Pull in live data with the shell
docs.text:
$(command) in a prompt is replaced by that command's output before the prompt is sent:

~/.prompts/commit_msg.md
Write a conventional commit message for this change:

$(git diff --staged)

aia --no-output commit_msg

See ERB and Shell Expansion.

docs.title: 6. Chat
docs.text:
Add --chat to keep the conversation going after the first answer, or start a chat with no prompt at all:

aia --chat

Entering interactive chat mode...
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Follow up (cntl-D or 'exit' to end) #=>
What's a good name for a CLI that converts CSV to JSON?

Inside a chat, lines that start with / are directives: /model, /include notes.md, /checkpoint, /help. See Chat Sessions.

docs.title: 7. Pick a model
docs.text:
aia --no-output --model claude-sonnet-4-5 explain lib/parser.rb
aia --available-models claude        # search the model catalog

See Choosing Models.

docs.title: 8. Ask several models at once
docs.text:
aia --no-output --model gpt-4o,claude-sonnet-4-5 explain lib/parser.rb

Each model answers in parallel. Add --consensus to have their answers merged into one. See Multiple Models and Consensus.

docs.title: 9. Put on a role
docs.text:
A role is a reusable persona stored in ~/.prompts/roles/:

cat > ~/.prompts/roles/reviewer.md <<'ROLE'
You are a meticulous senior code reviewer. Point out bugs first, then style.
ROLE

aia --no-output --role reviewer explain lib/parser.rb

See Roles and Skills.

docs.title: 10. See what it costs
docs.text:
aia --no-output --cost explain lib/parser.rb

After the response AIA prints a table of input/output tokens, elapsed time and cost. See Output, History and Usage.

docs.title: Where to go from here
docs.text:
You've now seen most of what AIA does day to day. Two good next steps:

  • Your First Prompt: build a real, reusable prompt step by step
  • Running Prompts: every way of telling AIA what to run

Later, when you want more: Pipelines, Tools, MCP Servers.

docs.title: Directives
docs.text: Directives are AIA's built-in commands. Some pull content into a prompt, such as a file, a web page or the clipboard. Others change settings, manage the conversation, or switch on a special mode for your next question. This page shows how to use them. Every directive is listed in the Directives Reference.

docs.title: Two ways to call a directive
docs.text:
A directive has the same name in both places, but you call it differently.

In chat: /nameIn a prompt file: ERB

During a chat session, type a slash, the directive's name and any arguments on a line by themselves:

Follow up (cntl-D or 'exit' to end) #=>
/temperature 0.2

Arguments are split on spaces. Quotes don't group words.

Inside a prompt file, call the directive as an ERB tag. Put string arguments in quotes:

Summarize the article below in three bullet points.

<%= webpage 'https://example.com/blog/release-notes' %>

The directive's result replaces the tag before the prompt is sent.

Type /help in a chat session to list every directive with its aliases.

docs.title: What happens to a directive's output in chat
docs.text:
Directives fall into three groups, and each group behaves differently in chat:

Kind Examples What happens Content /include, /insert, /webpage, /paste, /skill AIA prints the content and sends it to the model as part of the conversation, so you can ask about it next. Information and settings /help, /tools, /config, /model, /review, /cost AIA prints the result or makes the change. Nothing is sent to the model. Next-prompt modes /verify, /decompose, /debate, /spawn AIA confirms the mode. Your next message is handled in that mode, and then AIA returns to normal.

Only one next-prompt mode can be active at a time. If you request a second one before your next message, it replaces the first.

If you type a slash command AIA doesn't know, it replies Unknown directive: /foo (use /help to see available directives) and sends nothing to the model.

docs.title: Composing prompts from other files
docs.text:
include and insert let you build prompts from reusable pieces.

Directive What you get include 'file' The file is processed as a prompt: shell expansion, ERB and parameters all apply. Included files can include other files. insert 'file' (alias read) The file's text exactly as it is. Nothing is processed. 
---
parameters:
  code_file:
---
<%= include 'shared/review_guidelines.md' %>

Review this code:

<%= insert code_file %>

In a prompt file, paths are relative to the directory of the file that contains the tag. In chat, /include notes.md and /insert notes.md are relative to your current directory.

Note

include needs to know which file it is in, so it works in prompt files in your prompts directory and in chat. Use insert in executable prompts and in prompts piped on STDIN. If an include chain loops back to a file already being included, AIA stops with a circular-include error.

docs.title: Bringing in outside content
docs.text:
/webpage https://ruby-lang.org/en/news/      # fetch a page as Markdown
/paste                                       # whatever is on your clipboard
/skill changelog                             # the text of a skill
/skills                                      # list the skills you have

/webpage (aliases /website, /web) uses the pure.md service, and needs the PUREMD_API_KEY environment variable set.

docs.title: Settings during a chat
docs.text:
/model                     # show the current model(s)
/model claude-sonnet-4     # switch models and keep the conversation
/temperature 0.9           # also /temp
/top_p 0.5                 # also /topp
/config                    # show every setting
/config llm                # show one section
/config debug true         # change a setting
/cost                      # tokens and cost so far, as CSV

When you switch models with /model, the new model is given a summary of the conversation so far. Set model_switch_history to replay or clean to change that. See Choosing Models.

docs.title: Managing the conversation
docs.text:
/checkpoint before_refactor   # save a named point (also /ckp, /cp)
/checkpoints                  # list saved points
/review                       # show the conversation with checkpoint markers
/restore before_refactor      # go back; later messages are discarded
/clear                        # forget everything except the system prompt
/clear --all                  # forget the system prompt too

/restore with no name goes back to the checkpoint before the most recent one. See Chat Sessions.

docs.title: Special modes for the next prompt
docs.text:
/verify
Is 2^61 - 1 prime?

The /verify directive above gets two independent answers and then reconciles them. Others in this group are /decompose, /debate, /delegate, /concurrent, /orchestrate and /spawn. The crew directives /add_recruit, /drop_recruit and /reskill manage a team of robots that you can address with @name. These are covered in Advanced Modes and Crews.

docs.title: Looking around
docs.text:
/help          # all directives
/tools         # tools the model can call; /tools file narrows the list
/mcp           # MCP servers: connected, failed, and their tools
/robots        # the active robot(s): model, cost per 1K tokens, tools, role
/models gpt    # models whose names contain "gpt" (-term excludes)
/plugins       # loaded plugin files

docs.title: Running code
docs.text:
/ruby Date.today.cwday     # also /rb; needs --allow-ruby-eval
/say Build finished        # speak text aloud with the macOS say command

/ruby is off unless you start AIA with --allow-ruby-eval. See ERB & Shell.

docs.title: Which directives belong where
docs.text:
All directives can technically be called from both places, but most are designed for one of them:

  • In prompt files: include, insert, webpage, paste and skill. These are the directives that return text.
  • In chat: everything else. Settings belong in a prompt file's front matter, not in a /config call inside ERB.

docs.title: Writing your own directive
docs.text:
A custom directive is a small Ruby file. Load it with --tools, the same option that loads tools:

# ~/.prompts/tools/timestamp_directive.rb
module AIA
  class CustomDirectives < Directive
    desc "Insert current timestamp (optional strftime format)"
    def timestamp(args = [], context_manager = nil)
      format = args.empty? ? '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S' : args.join(' ')
      Time.now.strftime(format)
    end
  end
end

aia --tools ~/.prompts/tools/timestamp_directive.rb --chat

Now <%= timestamp %> works in prompt files, and /timestamp %Y-%m-%d works in chat. The desc line is required. It registers the method as a directive and supplies its /help text. The args value is the list of words that follow the directive name.

For helper methods that only your ERB templates need, a plugin is simpler.
